title: Batteries first - The Times of India
description:
From April to August, India imported nearly $3 billion worth of batteries from China.
This would make sense if using imported batteries helped India save as much money on oil and gas as it spent on batteries.
So, more electric cars mean more money spent on importing large batteries, without equal savings on oil and gas.
There is little point in reducing dependence on imported oil only to become more dependent on imported batteries.
India must make a big push to build the entire battery industry, from research and processing metals to making finished batteries.
text:
EVs are good, but India will save foreign exchange only when it can make its own batteries Last year, India spent about $135 billion on imported oil and gas, even though global prices were low. This year, the bill will be much higher because of the Iran war. Oil and gas are India’s biggest imports. If we can reduce these imports, it will become easier to protect the rupee. Electric vehicles (EVs) seem like a good solution. But, as TOI reported on Monday, they are increasing another import bill. From April to August, India imported nearly $3 billion worth of batteries from China. If this trend continues, the bill could reach $7 billion for the full year. This would make sense if using imported batteries helped India save as much money on oil and gas as it spent on batteries. But that is not always the case. According to a recent report by HSBC Global Research, batteries used in electric scooters, delivery vehicles, e-rickshaws and electric buses can pay for themselves in two to three years through savings on fuel. But electric cars take seven to eight years, on average, to recover their battery costs. This is because most cars are driven relatively little and spend much of their time parked. So, more electric cars mean more money spent on importing large batteries, without equal savings on oil and gas. Ironically, the government is offering large subsidies to encourage people to buy EVs. In Delhi, India’s biggest vehicle market, an expert panel has even recommended phasing out all petrol and diesel cars by 2040. Should India stop switching to electric vehicles? No. But it must work much harder to make batteries at home. West Asia is an important source of oil and gas, but India can buy these fuels from other countries, such as Russia, the US and Venezuela. China, however, has a very strong hold over the lithium battery market. This should make India think twice about becoming too dependent on it. India aims to build the capacity to make battery cells that can store 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy. Some Chinese factories can produce much more than that on their own. There is little point in reducing dependence on imported oil only to become more dependent on imported batteries. So far, India has made little progress in battery manufacturing. Batteries made here still use imported cells and electronic parts. Around this time last year, India's battery-making capacity was only 1.4 GWh. Demand for lithium batteries is growing rapidly, not just for EVs but also for energy storage systems and data centres. India must make a big push to build the entire battery industry, from research and processing metals to making finished batteries. We have built large oil refineries before, so we should be able to do this too.

The EU also plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 units a year starting in December, about half the current level.

With the U.S. and now the EU bolting the door against Chinese products, the Korean government has effectively done nothing.

text:
The European Union is erecting new regulatory barriers to defend its market from a Chinese electric-vehicle offensive. Germany and France have agreed that from 2028, subsidies and public procurement benefits within the 27-nation bloc will go only to vehicles that are assembled and developed in the EU and that generate more than 70% of the value of core components excluding batteries, foreign media reported on the 18th. The aim is to tighten the "Made in Europe" standard, a policy favoring manufacturing inside the bloc, in order to block Chinese EVs entering the European market through detours such as Turkey. The EU also plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 units a year starting in December, about half the current level.

The EU is raising its defenses because China, armed with prices roughly 20% lower than European models, is threatening the bloc's manufacturing base. Chinese eco-friendly vehicles account for 12% of new car sales in Europe and are rapidly taking market share. In the global EV market outside China, Chinese brands including BYD held a 22.8% share from January through August. The United States has already imposed tariffs of up to 127.5% since 2024 to protect its home market from China's EV push. The EU levies tariffs of up to 45.3%, but has concluded that duties alone are not enough.

With the U.S. and now the EU bolting the door against Chinese products, the Korean government has effectively done nothing. Tariffs on Chinese automobiles stand at just 8%, and taxpayer money is still handed out in purchase subsidies. Electric vehicles were also left out of the "Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act," which offers tax credits for domestic production in strategic industries. That leaves Korean companies defenseless against the export push by Chinese EV makers backed by massive state support. If this continues, the possibility cannot be ruled out that Korea's own EV market — of which 35% has already gone to Chinese brands — will be swallowed whole.

The auto industry is a core strategic sector that underpins exports and employment, with wide ripple effects on upstream and downstream businesses. If it falters, the entire economy will take a critical hit as the manufacturing base weakens and jobs disappear. To fend off China's relentless EV offensive and preserve the competitiveness of a Korean auto industry now at a crossroads, the most urgent task is to include electric and hybrid vehicles in the Korean version of the IRA being pursued by the government and the National Assembly.

text:
SULLIVAN COUNTY, Ind. — Amazon, American Electric Power and X-energy have agreed to explore building a nuclear power plant in southwest Indiana’s Sullivan County, on the site of a former coal plant.

The 12-unit plant would primarily power an Amazon Web Services data center cluster being developed and commissioned in the state, but power would also be transmitted over the grid, according to Benjamin Reinke, senior vice president for global business development at X-energy.

How the project would work

AEP would own and operate the plant. Amazon would pay for it. X-energy would supply the small modular reactors, known as SMRs, that would power it. “Which is extremely robust and the safest form of nuclear energy on earth,” Reinke said.

The project would benefit customers, not just the Amazon Web Services data center. Officials say the plant would add nearly 1 gigawatt of energy to the grid.

“Which is about the amount of power that 750 to 800 thousand American homes would use, so it’s a substantial amount of power,” Reinke said.

Jobs and rate impact

The nuclear investment could bring more than 1,000 construction jobs and over 100 permanent jobs to the area.

AEP says customers could see rate relief. Indiana Michigan Power plans to lower residential rates by $100 starting in 2027, and freeze them for three years.

“It’s a tri-party agreement where the three of us have the same goals to deploy more nuclear. Amazon is driving toward its net-zero carbon goal by 2040. AEP and their senior leadership want to deploy more nuclear because they see it as a clean, firm safe baseload,” said Brandon Oyer, director of energy and water for Amazon Web Services.

No approval yet

The agreement is only a partnership. There is no approval to build yet. If the project moves forward, construction would begin in the mid-2030s before the plant becomes operational.

text:
WRIGHTSTOWN, Wis. — The Public Service Commission of Wisconsin recently projected that the state's peak electricity demand will increase by over 40% by 2032. To support that expected need, the commission approved two southern Wisconsin natural gas plants last week.

State regulators approved Chicago-based Invenergy’s applications for the Foundry Ridge Energy Center in Walworth County and the Red Oak Ridge Energy Center in Kenosha County.

Invenergy is developing these natural gas projects for We Energies.

We Energies has also filed plans to construct a 750-megawatt natural gas plant at the Fox Energy Center in Wrightstown in Outagamie County.

That plan has those who oppose the project speaking out.

“This power plant is still going to release pollutants into the air,” Jayne Black said.

She’s concerned about We Energies' plans to build a 750-megawatt natural gas plant at its Fox Energy Center in Wrightstown. Black lives about 15 miles away from this proposed plant. She also works with the group Moms for Clean Air Force and is concerned about the plant’s emissions.

“Methane gas, fossil fuels, which is so harmful to people's health, and I'm especially concerned about our most vulnerable, and that's our children,” Black said.

We Energies has submitted a 31-page engineering plan to the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin.

It states the project is expected to exceed emission rates for several harmful gases, including nitrous oxide and carbon monoxide. To mitigate those emissions, the filing also stated that We Energies plans to install emissions control equipment and a continuous emissions monitoring system.

Jonathan Kim with the Energy and Policy Institute said his organization is concerned by the growing number of energy plant projects in the state.

“We have more than five gigawatts of new fossil gas generation proposed at this point over just the last year and a half,” Kim said.

Kim is a research manager with the group. Although We Energies did not say whether the Fox North Energy Center project is intended to serve artificial intelligence, Kim said the writing is on the wall.

“It's pretty clear this energy is going to be used for data centers. Utilities might try to obfuscate that fact, but that's where most of the demand for new electricity is coming from in Wisconsin,” Kim said.

In a statement to Spectrum News, We Energies spokesperson Brendan Conway said:

“The Fox North Energy Center will help meet Wisconsin's growing energy needs and strengthen grid reliability across the region. The engineering plan marks the first step in the review process. Additional information about the project will be provided through regulatory filings in the coming months.”

But Black cautions that meeting the state's energy demands should not come at the expense of Wisconsin's environment,

“Wisconsin has made a commitment to 100% clean energy by 2050, and every fossil fuel power plant sets us back,” Black said.

According to We Energies' engineering plan, the company expects to begin site development in 2029 and start plant operations by late 2032

text:
RICHMOND, VA — Governor Abigail Spanberger today — in expert testimony filed with the State Corporation Commission (SCC) on behalf of the Office of Governor — called on NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy to freeze residential electricity rates for six years and triple monthly customer bill credits as conditions of any merger.

The Governor urged the SCC to reject the proposed $67 billion merger in the absence of these and other guarantees and additional binding commitments to protect and preserve Virginia jobs, lower energy costs for families, and accelerate Virginia’s progress toward producing affordable, reliable, local, and clean power into the future.

“Any proposed merger involving Virginia’s primary state-regulated utility must benefit families, small businesses, and Virginia’s workforce — not just the shareholders of these multi-billion-dollar corporations,” said Governor Abigail Spanberger. “That’s why I am calling for a six-year freeze to Virginians’ base residential electricity rates, a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers, and additional commitments to lower energy costs and meet our long-term clean and homegrown energy goals if the State Corporation Commission is to approve this merger.”

Governor Spanberger continued, “As Governor, I will continue to advocate aggressively on behalf of Virginians over the coming months, and I remain deeply skeptical that the proposed $67 billion merger, as currently structured, will adequately protect consumers and deliver meaningful public benefits. Without enforceable commitments that meaningfully prioritize ratepayers, lower energy costs, protect Virginia’s utility workforce, and advance Virginia’s energy goals, the State Corporation Commission should reject this merger.”

As a condition of approving this transaction, the Governor is also calling for additional commitments to put Virginia’s families, workers, and ratepayers first. These include reforms to lower the share of costs borne by residential customers, stronger protections against utility disconnections for Virginians, and greater investments in energy efficiency and locally generated clean energy.

The Governor is also seeking structural reforms to ensure large data centers bear the cost of their own energy needs — not families — and expand rooftop solar by eliminating the program’s cap. Critically, these commitments must be backed by strong enforcement provisions from the SCC that hold these companies accountable for their promises to Virginians and their workers.

“With the commitments made in the original filing and supplemental testimony, Dominion and NextEra have not yet satisfied the legal standard that would allow the Commission to approve this transaction,” said Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond. “This testimony lays out the bold actions that will be required in this transformative moment to ensure just and reasonable rates for Virginia customers resulting from the proposed merger.”

Dr. Richard McCann — a leading expert on energy, water, and environmental policy — provided expert testimony on behalf of Governor Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Allmond. Dr. McCann has consulted on environmental and energy resource economics and policy since 1985, testifying more than 50 times before numerous regulatory agencies as well as in trial and arbitration cases. Dr. McCann also testified before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the California Energy Crisis Refund Proceeding.

In August, Governor Spanberger formally filed a Notice of Participation as Respondent, becoming the first Governor of Virginia to intervene at the SCC. The Governor announced her decision to intervene in the proposed merger in a Washington Post op-ed — laying out three non-negotiable priorities: delivering more affordable energy bills for Virginians, protecting Virginia’s utility workforce, and accelerating Virginia’s progress toward producing affordable, reliable, local, and clean power into the future.

As a party to the case, the Governor and her Administration have the legal right to engage, bring concerns forward, request detailed information about the proposed merger, and make clear that Virginians expect to see long-term, tangible benefits of any potential deal.

Read below for a summary of the filing with the State Corporation Commission.

—

Summary of the Direct Testimony of Richard McCann on behalf of Governor Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Allmond

My testimony evaluates the Joint Petition to determine whether the commitments made will ensure that “just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized” and are otherwise in the public interest. I conclude that the Joint Petitioners, through the commitments made in the Joint Petition and Supplemental Testimony, have not yet met that standard.

In order for the Commission to approve the proposed transaction, the following additional ratepayer-related commitments should be made:

Residential Rate Freeze for Six Years: There cannot be an increase to base rates for three rate case cycles.

Triple Ratepayer Benefit: This would make the rebate $29 per month for four years.

Fixing Dominion’s Capital Structure: The debt share in Dominion’s capital structure must be increased from 48% to 60% to reduce the Company’s rate of return.

Requiring the “Probability of Dispatch” Method: This change reduces the residential share of relevant costs by 25%.

Improved Disconnection Policies: Extend disconnection protections to households with infants, those with serious medical conditions or inability to pay due to financial hardship, and during high Air Quality Index days.

In order for the Commission to approve the proposed transaction, the following additional clean energy-related commitments should be made:

Energy Efficiency and Distributed Energy Resources Prioritization: Energy Efficiency and distributed energy resources must be designated as the first priorities for meeting forecasted loads in all resource planning and acquisition activities.

Formation of a Zero-Carbon Energy Generation Company: A new separate subsidiary must be created and headquartered in Virginia for building zero-carbon energy generation to serve large data centers that is financially walled off from the rest of customers.

Creation of a State Energy Efficiency Utility: An independent energy efficiency utility should be recommended to the General Assembly to meet our energy efficiency goals.

Decarbonization Incentive Rate: A decarbonization incentive rate must be established for electrified uses like heat pumps to replace furnaces and electric vehicles to replace fossil-fueled cars.

Eliminating Rooftop Solar Cap: The elimination of the cap on the net metering program should be recommended to the General Assembly to spur more local energy generation.

Mandatory, Comprehensive Enforceability provisions must be imposed to hold the Joint Petitioners fully accountable for any violation of commitments, including the labor and workforce commitments.

Unless these additional commitments are substantially addressed or alternative solutions are identified, the Commission should reject the joint petition.

—

text:
Louisiana politics doesn’t leave much room for ideological purity, at least not if you’re serious about getting things done. That is one reason Big Easy Magazine is endorsing Congressman Troy Carter. We can hold strong progressive values while recognizing that the policies we support have real consequences for working families. And sometimes getting something accomplished means working with members of Louisiana’s Republican congressional delegation, many of whom are closely aligned with Trump, even when their politics are antithetical to our values.

Carter belongs to the Congressional Progressive Caucus, but he’s also part of the New Democrat Coalition, which tends to put more emphasis on economic growth and bipartisan cooperation. Some might find that contradictory. I think it reflects the reality of representing a state like Louisiana, where progressive reforms often have to compete with powerful and influential corporate interests.

In September, Carter helped get the TWICE Act through the House alongside Republican Congressman Clay Higgins. Anyone familiar with Higgins’ politics knows these two aren’t exactly ideological neighbors.

The legislation addresses a problem that has probably kept more than a few people from finding work after prison. Louisiana has plenty of jobs in maritime transportation and related industries that require a Transportation Worker Identification Credential, commonly called a TWIC card. Carter’s bill would help eligible incarcerated people begin figuring out that application process before they’re released, without weakening the existing security requirements.

We spend years talking about rehabilitation and giving people second chances, but someone can leave prison ready to work and immediately run into another bureaucratic obstacle. The bill passed the House on September 16. It still needs Senate approval, but that’s meaningful progress.

I would much rather see Congress spending time on legislation like this than another round of political theater. People are hurting right now. Carter prioritizes results over politics, even when doing so means working with people with whom he disagrees.

Our endorsement certainly doesn’t mean we agree with Carter on everything. Environmental policy is probably the best example. But even here, there is an argument that his approach has been pragmatic rather than dismissive.

Environmental justice groups in the River Parishes have spent years voicing concern about pollution from nearby petrochemical facilities. Some have called for an end to new industrial development in communities already surrounded by these plants. Carter hasn’t gone that far, and it’s no secret that he sees the energy and chemical industries as important parts of Louisiana’s economy. But we can’t flip a switch overnight and transform an economy that has depended on these industries for generations.

He’s also supported policies designed to mitigate the pollution these communities are up against. His Public Health Air Quality Act would expand community-level air monitoring and improve public access to pollution data. Groups including RISE St. James and the Louisiana Bucket Brigade have supported the legislation. Carter criticized the federal government’s decision to drop its Clean Air Act case against the Denka facility in St. John the Baptist Parish and later helped introduce the ZELDIN Act to strengthen oversight of certain EPA decisions.

Black and Brown communities have been disproportionately impacted by the pollution and have fought for decades for meaningful change. However, the congressman knows we can’t seriously discuss Louisiana’s environmental future without dealing with its economic dependence on these industries. We are not going to persuade a plant worker in St. Charles Parish earning a good living that his job needs to disappear for the greater good. At the same time, a family living beside a chemical facility shouldn’t be expected to accept dangerous pollution because the plant happens to provide good jobs.

We’ve spent far too long treating those concerns as though one has to cancel out the other. To address climate change, Louisiana must enact policies that will incentivize cleaner industries to invest in our state. Our congressman must continue to prioritize both environmental protection and economic opportunity.

Though Carter hasn’t solved that problem yet, we have witnessed an honest and genuine effort to address the environmental inequities and injustices these communities continue to face.

His seat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee gives him an opportunity to influence how those decisions are made. That same willingness to work through complicated policy questions shows up in other areas of Carter’s recent work, including some that don’t get nearly as much attention in Louisiana politics.

For instance, he recently joined Congressman Bennie Thompson in reintroducing legislation to establish an artificial intelligence security task force within the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. He has argued that government needs to address the cybersecurity and national security risks associated with AI without unnecessarily restricting innovation. Technology is moving quickly, and Congress hasn’t exactly demonstrated an ability to keep up.

Congress has struggled to keep up in other areas too, including mental health care. Carter also joined California Congresswoman Doris Matsui on legislation to expand workforce training and support for professionals working in the 988 crisis-response system. Carter has recognized the growing mental health care crisis in this country, one made worse by housing instability, financial stress and the pressures facing working- and middle-class families.

Carter’s work on health care also goes back beyond the current Congress. In 2022, he voted for the PACT Act, which became law and significantly expanded health care and disability benefits for veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic substances. His district office has held VA resource events to help local veterans navigate disability claims and other benefits.

We get it. With a Republican-controlled Congress, these proposals are not law. Neither party has been able to advance enough meaningful legislation in the current political environment. Still, they address problems that deserve more attention than they’re getting, and if Democrats take back control of the House, some of Carter’s proposals could have a clearer path through committee and onto the House floor.

While some of those proposals address national problems, Carter has also stayed focused on issues that hit much closer to home. In September, he joined Republican Mike Ezell and Democrat Bennie Thompson in introducing legislation requiring FEMA to develop more comprehensive staffing and disaster-response plans. He’s co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Flood Resilience Caucus, which challenged proposed changes to the National Flood Insurance Program that could make coverage even more expensive.

Insurance costs have become a serious threat to homeownership in Louisiana. New Orleans in particular has continued to lose population in recent years. Families are struggling to afford their mortgages because of skyrocketing premiums. Carter is able to set aside his political ideology to work with Louisiana’s Republican delegation, because flood insurance and disaster response are not issues where refusing to work together accomplishes anything.

Carter has brought substantial federal funding back to his district. In 2024 alone, he secured $17.5 million in Community Project Funding for projects that included Lincoln Beach access and wastewater improvements in Gretna. He also supported the bipartisan infrastructure law that helped provide $300 million in federal grants for the Port of New Orleans’ planned Louisiana International Terminal. More recently, he helped secure additional funding for Xavier and Ochsner’s medical school development and other local infrastructure projects that included the New Orleans Public Belt Railroad.

In September, FEMA extended the deadline for roughly $38 million in federally funded repairs to the Morris F.X. Jeff Sr. Municipal Auditorium through February 2028. Carter was among the officials pushing for the extension. He wasn’t alone, and these projects rarely happen because of one elected official. But keeping federal funding available for New Orleans is part of representing the district, and it deserves recognition.

Carter’s work lately has not been limited to bringing home federal money or dealing with the everyday problems of governing. He has also become increasingly vocal about something much bigger: who gets political power in Louisiana and across the South.

After the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, Carter spoke out against efforts that could leave Louisiana with only one majority-Black congressional district instead of two. That fight connects to a broader argument he’s been making about the political future of the South.

Carter has repeatedly said that “All Roads Lead Through the South,” including during a recent appearance on MSNOW. He has argued that Democrats have largely treated the South as politically hopeless despite its large Black population and the potential to build stronger coalitions across Southern communities.

He also believes efforts to weaken Black voting power could have the opposite effect by motivating more people to get politically involved.

National Democrats have spent years pouring resources into a relatively small number of competitive states while much of the South receives considerably less attention. That approach may make sense when you’re looking at one election cycle, but it doesn’t do much to build a lasting political presence. Congressman Carter recognizes that in order to win in places like Louisiana, we must be able to organize and give people reasons to believe their participation matters. And as first vice chair of the Congressional Black Caucus, he’s in a position to keep making that case nationally.

I don’t agree with every position Carter has taken, nor do I think the legislation he’s introduced should automatically be treated as an accomplishment simply because it has his name attached. There are also legitimate questions about whether his environmental policies go far enough, and those disagreements shouldn’t disappear just because someone supports him politically.

But when I look at his record, I see a congressman willing to work with Republicans when there’s something worthwhile to accomplish without backing away from issues such as voting rights and environmental justice.

There are plenty of issues where I want Carter to push harder. But I also appreciate that he understands something too many people in politics seem to forget. Sometimes you have to work with people you can’t stand to get something done.

We need people willing to fight for progressive causes, but we also need representatives who understand the economic realities of the state they’re representing. Progressive rhetoric without results is futile.

There will be decisions worth criticizing, and I fully expect there will be areas where we push him to do more. But looking at the work he’s done, particularly over the last several months, I believe he’s earned the opportunity to continue representing Louisiana’s Second Congressional District. With the issues we continue to face, now is not the time for on-the-job training.

That’s why Big Easy Magazine is endorsing Troy Carter.

title: OAL Approves CARB's Initial Regulation, Locking In November 10, 2026 SB 253 Reporting Deadline
authors: Jon Solorzano, Kelly Rondinelli, Chloe Schmergel, Alyssa Sieja, Josh Rutenberg
description:
On October 12, 2026, the California Office of Administrative Law (“OAL”) approved the California Air Resources Board’s (“CARB”) California Corporate Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Initial Regulation (the “Initial Regulation”).
With that approval, administrative review is complete and November 10, 2026, is formally set as the first-year deadline for reporting Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions under SB 253.
On February 26, 2026, CARB approved the Initial Regulation implementing SB 253 and its companion law, the California Climate-Related Financial Risk Act (“SB 261”).
Reporting entities can submit their reports through CARB’s voluntary 2026 Report Intake Platform or by email.
While reporting under SB 253 now appears more certain than ever, constitutional challenges to this law and SB 261 remain pending, and an injunction could halt the reporting requirements.
text:
On October 12, 2026, the California Office of Administrative Law (“OAL”) approved the California Air Resources Board’s (“CARB”) California Corporate Greenhouse Gas Reporting and Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Initial Regulation (the “Initial Regulation”). The regulation took effect the same day. With that approval, administrative review is complete and November 10, 2026, is formally set as the first-year deadline for reporting Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions under SB 253. As we have previously written, the November 10, 2026 deadline was anticipated, but barring an injunction from the Ninth Circuit relating to pending litigation on SB 253 and its sister law, SB 261 (more on this below), this leaves covered companies less than a month to file their first reports. The Initial Regulation also establishes CARB’s fee program and defines key terms such as “revenue” and “doing business in California.”

Background

The California Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act (“SB 253”) requires U.S.-based companies that have more than $1 billion in annual revenue and are “doing business” in California to disclose their Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 GHG emissions each year. On February 26, 2026, CARB approved the Initial Regulation implementing SB 253 and its companion law, the California Climate-Related Financial Risk Act (“SB 261”). CARB sent the regulatory package to OAL on May 20. As we reported in June, CARB then withdrew it from OAL review on June 23 so it could move the first-year deadline back three months, from August 10 to November 10, 2026, to give reporting entities more time to absorb the final rules. Following a 15-day public comment period from July 27 to August 11, CARB resubmitted the final package to OAL on September 21 with only a handful of additional non-substantive changes. Notably, approval of the Initial Regulation does not change the litigation landscape; SB 261 remains subject to a preliminary injunction issued by the Ninth Circuit, and that injunction does not, for now, extend to SB 253. The parties have since notified the Ninth Circuit of the OAL approval by letter under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 28(j).

Key Developments

The Initial Regulation is now codified at Title 17, California Code of Regulations, sections 96070–96077, formalizing the November 10 deadline. Upon OAL’s approval, CARB announced that it sent a “reminder letter” (posted on its website on October 9) to entities it has identified as potentially subject to SB 253. However, do not treat receipt of such a letter, or the lack of one, as an official determination of whether a company is within the scope of the reporting requirements. This is merely a notification that CARB has identified such entities as presumptively in scope based on the agency’s records or other public information indicating a likely sufficient nexus to the laws. Entities may still be subject to the reporting requirements, even if they did not receive a reminder letter, and certain entities receiving the letter may determine that they are not subject to the reporting requirements (in which case no action is required).

As we previously discussed, CARB has published guidance to assist reporting entities in the preparation and submission of their first reports. That guidance provides a level of flexibility for companies preparing their initial reports, including with respect to the specific emission factor dataset companies elect to use. Pursuant to that guidance, companies can satisfy the 2026 requirement by submitting an existing annual report that includes Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, data already reported to other programs, or CARB’s optional template, and third-party assurance is not required this year. Reporting entities can submit their reports through CARB’s voluntary 2026 Report Intake Platform or by email. As a reminder, companies that were not collecting, and were not planning to collect, Scope 1 or Scope 2 GHG emissions information on or before December 5, 2024, may instead submit a statement of non-reporting on company letterhead for the 2026 cycle.

Takeaways

The reporting deadline is no longer a moving target. Companies that may be subject to SB 253 should confirm their reporting status and, if SB 253 is applicable, finalize their fiscal year 2025 Scope 1 and Scope 2 data to submit by November 10.1 Companies relying on CARB’s first-year enforcement flexibility should keep in mind that it does not eliminate the reporting obligation. Those entities should document their good-faith compliance efforts and follow CARB’s submission guidance.

The 2026 cycle is only the first step. CARB has said that a separate rulemaking will address reporting for 2027 and later years, including Scope 3 disclosures and independent third-party assurance. At a July 21 workshop, CARB previewed proposals that would largely follow the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, phase in five Scope 3 categories beginning in 2027, and require limited third-party assurance of Scope 1 and Scope 2 data, so companies should anticipate the need to develop supporting data and controls. While reporting under SB 253 now appears more certain than ever, constitutional challenges to this law and SB 261 remain pending, and an injunction could halt the reporting requirements. This, however, is far from guaranteed. Companies should thus assume that the reporting requirements will proceed as planned and November 10, 2026, is a firm deadline. V&E is monitoring these developments closely and will provide updates going forward as CARB’s 2027 rulemaking moves ahead.

We will continue to track developments related to California’s climate reporting laws. Please reach out to your Vinson & Elkins team to discuss these matters and their implications for your business.

title: China vs US vs Europe vs India: Who Leads Clean-Tech Manufacturing in 2026? Major ...
description:
Major Chinese clean-tech manufacturing projects CATL – Lithium-ion battery manufacturing CATL operates major battery manufacturing facilities in Ningde, Yibin and other Chinese industrial locations.
Europe Expands EV Battery Manufacturing Despite Cost Challenges Europe is developing domestic battery production to reduce reliance on imported cells and strengthen its automotive manufacturing industry.
India Emerges as a Solar and Battery Manufacturing Challenger India is expanding clean-tech manufacturing through solar production, battery gigafactories and government-supported industrial programmes.
By June 2026, cumulative manufacturing capacity reached 261.7 GW for solar modules and 36.6 GW for solar cells, according to India’s solar manufacturing capacity assessment.
The United States is expanding domestic solar and battery production through major investments by First Solar, Qcells and Toyota.
text:
China continues to dominate global clean-tech manufacturing in 2026, while the United States, Europe and India are investing billions of dollars in solar panels, electric vehicle (EV) batteries, energy-storage systems and wind equipment. Major manufacturing projects by CATL, BYD, First Solar, Qcells, Toyota, Volkswagen, Reliance Industries and Tata Group demonstrate the growing competition for industrial leadership.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the global market for key clean-energy technologies reached nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025. However, annual manufacturing investment declined from nearly $220 billion in 2023 to below $200 billion in 2024.

The competition is increasingly determined by factory output, manufacturing costs, supply-chain integration, technology and exports rather than investment announcements alone.

China Leads Global EV Battery and Solar Manufacturing

China remains the world’s largest clean-tech manufacturing hub, supported by integrated supply chains, extensive production capacity and competitive manufacturing costs.

According to the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026, China manufactured approximately 16 million electric cars in 2025, representing nearly 75 percent of global production. Chinese electric-car exports exceeded 2.5 million vehicles.

China also accounted for more than 80 percent of global battery-cell production, approximately 85 percent of cathode active-material production and more than 90 percent of anode active-material production.

Major Chinese clean-tech manufacturing projects

CATL – Lithium-ion battery manufacturing

CATL operates major battery manufacturing facilities in Ningde, Yibin and other Chinese industrial locations. Its manufacturing network supplies batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and stationary energy storage.

CATL’s extensive production capacity and investment in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology strengthen China’s position in global battery supply chains.

BYD – Integrated EV and battery manufacturing

BYD manufactures electric vehicles, Blade batteries, power electronics and other automotive components. Its vertically integrated operations reduce dependence on external suppliers and support manufacturing efficiency.

LONGi Green Energy – Solar manufacturing

LONGi produces solar wafers, cells and modules, including high-efficiency photovoltaic technologies. Its integrated manufacturing capabilities support China’s domestic solar market and international exports.

JinkoSolar – Solar cells and modules

JinkoSolar operates large-scale solar manufacturing facilities in China and international markets, producing photovoltaic wafers, cells and modules.

China’s main challenge is overcapacity, particularly in solar manufacturing, where aggressive pricing has weakened margins despite strong global demand.

United States Invests Billions in Solar and Battery Factories

The United States is expanding domestic clean-tech manufacturing through investments in solar modules, battery cells and advanced energy-storage technologies.

First Solar: $1.1 Billion Alabama Solar Factory

First Solar invested approximately $1.1 billion in its Alabama manufacturing facility, adding 3.5 GW of annual thin-film solar module capacity.

The factory, commissioned in September 2024, directly employed approximately 855 workers during 2025.

First Solar’s cadmium telluride technology differentiates its products from conventional crystalline-silicon solar modules manufactured predominantly in Asia.

Qcells: 8.4 GW Solar Module Manufacturing in Georgia

Hanwha Qcells expanded its manufacturing operations in Georgia, with its Cartersville facility beginning solar-cell production in June 2026.

The company’s integrated manufacturing programme targets 3.3 GW each of ingot, wafer and solar-cell capacity.

Together, Qcells’ Cartersville and Dalton facilities have approximately 8.4 GW of annual solar-module manufacturing capacity, supporting a workforce approaching 4,000 employees.

The investment is intended to strengthen domestic solar supply chains and reduce dependence on imported photovoltaic components.

Toyota: $13.9 Billion North Carolina Battery Factory

Toyota began production at its $13.9 billion battery manufacturing facility in Liberty, North Carolina, in 2025.

The factory covers approximately 7 million square feet and is designed to accommodate 14 battery production lines.

The facility will manufacture batteries for hybrid, plug-in hybrid and battery-electric vehicles, with planned employment reaching approximately 5,100.

Toyota’s investment demonstrates the growing importance of localized battery production for the US automotive industry.

Tesla: Battery and Energy Storage Manufacturing

Tesla operates battery manufacturing facilities in Nevada and Texas, alongside Megapack energy-storage system production in Lathrop, California.

These operations support electric vehicle production and utility-scale battery storage, two important segments of the US clean-tech market.

Europe Expands EV Battery Manufacturing Despite Cost Challenges

Europe is developing domestic battery production to reduce reliance on imported cells and strengthen its automotive manufacturing industry.

However, European manufacturers face higher electricity, labor and financing costs than many Asian competitors.

The IEA estimates that manufacturing efficiency accounts for more than 40 percent of the battery-cell production-cost difference between China and Europe.

Volkswagen PowerCo: 40 GWh Battery Factory in Germany

Volkswagen’s PowerCo commissioned battery-cell production at Salzgitter, Germany, in December 2025.

The first expansion stage targets 20 GWh of annual production capacity, sufficient for approximately 250,000 electric vehicles, depending on battery size.

The factory has the potential to expand to 40 GWh annually.

Its manufacturing building covers approximately 69,000 square metres. PowerCo also plans to replicate its standardized battery factory design in Spain and Canada.

ACC: Battery Manufacturing in France

Automotive Cells Company (ACC), backed by Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz and TotalEnergies, has developed battery-cell manufacturing at Billy-Berclau/Douvrin in France.

The facility supports European automotive manufacturers seeking regional battery supplies.

Verkor: Dunkirk Battery Gigafactory

French battery manufacturer Verkor is developing production capacity at Dunkirk to supply electric vehicle manufacturers.

The investment forms part of Europe’s broader effort to establish competitive battery manufacturing and reduce dependence on Asian suppliers.

Europe also retains strengths in wind turbine manufacturing, power electronics and electrical equipment through companies such as Siemens Gamesa, Vestas and Siemens Energy.

India Emerges as a Solar and Battery Manufacturing Challenger

India is expanding clean-tech manufacturing through solar production, battery gigafactories and government-supported industrial programmes.

During the first half of 2026, India added 50.6 GW of solar-module manufacturing capacity and 9.7 GW of solar-cell capacity.

By June 2026, cumulative manufacturing capacity reached 261.7 GW for solar modules and 36.6 GW for solar cells, according to India’s solar manufacturing capacity assessment.

The difference between module and cell capacity highlights India’s continued dependence on upstream photovoltaic components.

Reliance Industries: 20 GW Solar and 100 GWh Battery Ambitions

Reliance Industries is developing an integrated clean-energy manufacturing complex covering more than 5,000 acres at Jamnagar, Gujarat.

Its manufacturing programme includes:

20 GWp of targeted annual integrated solar manufacturing capacity.

An initial 40 GWh battery manufacturing phase, with longer-term ambitions reaching 100 GWh annually.

Electrolyser manufacturing designed for scalability to 3 GW annually.

These figures represent development targets rather than confirmed full-scale production.

Reliance aims to integrate solar, batteries and hydrogen-related technologies within its clean-energy manufacturing ecosystem.

Tata Agratas: 20 GWh Battery Factory in Gujarat

Tata Group’s Agratas is constructing a battery-cell manufacturing facility at Sanand, Gujarat.

The project occupies approximately 320 acres, with its first phase targeting 20 GWh of annual battery capacity and production planned for 2027.

In April 2026, Agratas reported completion of the structural steel frame.

The main building spans approximately 105,000 square metres, with more than 24,000 tonnes of steel deployed and peak construction employment exceeding 2,500 workers.

Waaree Energies, Adani Solar and Vikram Solar

Waaree Energies, Adani Solar and Vikram Solar are expanding India’s photovoltaic manufacturing ecosystem.

Their investments support solar modules, cells and higher-efficiency photovoltaic technologies, helping India develop domestic manufacturing capabilities.

However, competitive wafer, polysilicon and equipment supply remains essential for reducing import dependence.

Clean-Tech Manufacturing Projects: Investment and Capacity Comparison

Note: GW and GWh represent different measures of manufacturing capacity and are not directly comparable. Planned capacity is distinguished from operational output.

Who Will Lead Clean-Tech Manufacturing by 2030?

China remains the strongest global clean-tech manufacturing economy, combining production scale, integrated supply chains and established export markets.

The United States is expanding domestic solar and battery production through major investments by First Solar, Qcells and Toyota. Europe is strengthening battery manufacturing through Volkswagen PowerCo, ACC and Verkor.

India is emerging as a manufacturing challenger, supported by investments from Reliance Industries, Tata Group and leading solar manufacturers.

The IEA Energy Technology Perspectives 2026 identifies supply-chain concentration and manufacturing competitiveness as important factors shaping the industry’s future.

By 2030, leadership will depend on actual production, factory utilization, manufacturing costs, domestic value addition and export profitability.

text:
A federal patent lawsuit filed in East Texas indicates that massive quantities of Chinese crystal-pulling equipment are bound for Texas to build out a 10 GW solar production line.

Court filings and public records tie the multi-hundred-million-dollar machinery deal to Tesla’s planned $10.1 billion vertically integrated solar gigafactory in Fort Bend County, highlighting the U.S. solar industry’s continued reliance on imported heavy machinery to establish domestic ingot and wafer manufacturing.

Linton Crystal Technologies, an equipment maker based in Rochester, New York, filed a patent infringement complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas against Chinese machinery manufacturer Zhejiang Jingsheng Mechanical and Electrical, known as JSG.

The legal dispute centers on high-precision industrial furnaces called Czochralski crystal pullers. The machines melt raw silicon and grow monocrystalline silicon ingots, which are subsequently sliced into thin wafers to make solar cells. Ingot pulling represents the foundational first step in the entire solar manufacturing chain.

What the lawsuit claims

Linton alleges that JSG infringed on its patented designs for specialized seed-lifting and rotating systems used inside high-temperature crystal pullers. The systems carefully regulate the growing silicon crystal as it is drawn out of the molten material to ensure uniform structure and diameter.

According to the court complaint, Linton and JSG competed directly to supply crystal-growth furnaces for a major photovoltaic project in the United States.

Linton claims JSG secured the supply contract by utilizing contested designs and subsequently began importing the hardware into the country.

To establish personal jurisdiction in Texas, Linton cites public market reports showing that JSG secured a massive contract to supply crystal pullers and associated equipment for a 10 GW photovoltaic production line in Texas, with deliveries scheduled in 2026.

Potential connection to Tesla

Although Tesla is not named as a defendant in the litigation, the location, equipment scale, and delivery timelines match public regulatory filings for Project Crystal Sun, Tesla’s proposed $10.1 billion vertically integrated solar cell and module factory in Fort Bend County, Texas.

Recent local regulatory proceedings show that the local school board approved property tax incentives for the massive project footprint. The filings outline an $8.6 billion capital commitment specifically earmarked for manufacturing equipment and personal property. Unlike standard assembly facilities that simply wire imported cells into finished panels, equipment lists for the Texas project detail comprehensive machinery for upstream ingot pulling, wafer slicing, chemical coating, and automated cell fabrication.

Industry context

The litigation highlights the intense competitive pressures surrounding upstream machinery as developers race to build domestic solar wafer and cell production lines. While U.S. manufacturing incentives and domestic content rules encourage fully localized supply chains, the specialized heavy hardware required for ingot and wafer manufacturing remains heavily reliant on global equipment suppliers.

Neither Linton, JSG, nor Tesla immediately responded to requests for comment regarding the litigation. The case, Linton Crystal Technologies Corp. v. Zhejiang Jingsheng Mechanical and Electrical Co., Ltd., is pending before U.S. District Judge Rodney Gilstrap in the Marshall Division of the Eastern District of Texas.

text:
This story was originally published on Trucking Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Trucking Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

Southern California-based Ability Tri-Modal Transportation Services is working to convert 20 diesel tractors with swappable batteries through a partnership with Janus Electric, EVP Mike Kelso told Trucking Dive in a video interview Oct. 9.

The upgrades will allow an initial pair of trucks to run as battery-electric vehicles, he said, with two more conversions expected afterward. The batteries can be swapped out within minutes when a fully charged setup is needed.

"These were the first two that have ever been done in the U.S.," Founder and COO Lex Forsyth of Australia-headquartered Janus Electric said during a joint interview about Ability Tri-Modal's pending conversions. Toronto-based battery manufacturer Electrovaya is doing final testing of the packs and is about two weeks away from completion, he said.

Dive Insight:

Charging for heavy-duty electric trucks can be timely, but Janus Electric's approach seeks to save time and repurpose existing assets.

Ability Tri-Modal, headquartered near Los Angeles in Carson, already had two Freightliner eCascadia's, which the carrier introduced in 2023 and been in place amid California's sky-high diesel prices, which have averaged over $8 per gallon statewide in recent weeks.

While batteries are the most expensive part of the upgrades, the carrier won't need two battery packs for every one truck. Instead, in this use case, the carrier will only need a ratio of 1.1 batteries per trucks because the charging only takes three hours, Forsyth said.

"In the full 20 truck program, they're looking at 26 sets of batteries," Forsyth said.

Each conversion costs about $175,000, but through California's Clean Truck and Bus Voucher Incentive Project, known as HVIP, the price is reduced by $112,000, Kelso previously said in a LinkedIn video.

The remaining conversions could take about six to eight months, Forsyth said.

The tractors will have a range of about 300 miles, according to the companies. With the upgrade, a truck will have about 560 kilowatts of usable battery energy and get about 1.8 kilowatt hours to the miles, Forsyth said.

Janus Electric provides estimated ranges on worst-case scenarios, but carriers can improve that range based on how drivers operate the vehicle's regenerative braking. With that process, drivers lift their feet off accelerators, and a portion of electrical power is recovered back in the battery.

In Australia, most drayage operators using Janus Electric get about a 20% or 25% recovery in regen braking, Forsyth said.

"Depending on driver habits and and driver behavior, you can extend that range with regen braking," he said.

title: This geothermal startup produced a tiny bit of power from the seafloor - Canary Media
description:
The startup Endurance Energy deployed its test unit, called Adélie, about a mile below the surface of the Pacific Ocean during a three-week demonstration in September.
On Monday, the Seattle-based company announced the results, which it says mark a milestone for the world’s emerging and highly uncertain efforts to develop offshore geothermal power.
“We follow the adage ​‘make it exist, then make it good,’” said Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy.
The Adélie test is perhaps the most far-flung example of the growing push to expand America’s geothermal power capacity using next-generation technologies and in less-conventional locations.
Existing offshore geothermal initiatives have primarily focused on conducting research, not chasing commercial power.
text:
A tiny power plant notched a big win last month off the coast of Oregon: For nearly 30 seconds, it generated electricity using the heat of an underwater volcano.

The startup Endurance Energy deployed its test unit, called Adélie, about a mile below the surface of the Pacific Ocean during a three-week demonstration in September. On Monday, the Seattle-based company announced the results, which it says mark a milestone for the world’s emerging and highly uncertain efforts to develop offshore geothermal power.

“We follow the adage ​‘make it exist, then make it good,’” said Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy. ​“Adélie made it exist, and now we know it’s possible.”

Redd, who is a former SpaceX engineer, launched the startup in January 2025 with the goal of scaling a clean, always-on energy source. The company has since raised $63 million from an array of venture capital firms and is partnering with the Kingdom of Tonga on a plan to deploy a 2-megawatt project that would help reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel.

First, though, the Endurance team needs to ensure its technology can run for more than half a minute.

The Adélie test is perhaps the most far-flung example of the growing push to expand America’s geothermal power capacity using next-generation technologies and in less-conventional locations. While most everyone else is focused on harnessing heat terrestrially, Redd said he sees the most promise in the volcanically active regions where tectonic plates are spreading apart.

“It’s an eyebrow-raising approach,” said Emily Pope, a geologist and senior fellow at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions.

She said that while offshore geothermal is intriguing from a scientific perspective, it’s hard to see how projects could pencil out economically, given the cost and complexity of operating in harsh, salty ocean conditions and the long distances the power would have to travel to reach customers. Remote island nations, seemingly ideal candidates for the technology, could far more easily adopt lower-cost solar power and batteries to meet their energy needs.

“It is adding so much technological challenge to an energy production technology, without there being a really significant demand for it,” Pope said of the subsea pursuit.

Existing offshore geothermal initiatives have primarily focused on conducting research, not chasing commercial power. In 2016, a team of Chinese scientists produced a few watts of sustained power from a hydrothermal vent where the southwest Indian Ocean meets the southeast Atlantic Ocean. In southwest Iceland, a government-backed project drilled a geothermal well near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, but corrosive seawater caused major engineering hurdles.

Redd said Endurance differs from earlier initiatives. The company aims to operate at a far greater scale and is designing technology ​“from scratch” to survive the intense pressure and corrosiveness of the deep sea, including by using a lot of titanium.

The Adélie expedition began last month aboard the Ocean Guardian vessel, which sailed about 300 miles west of Oregon to the Axial Seamount, an active submarine volcano along the Juan de Fuca Ridge. The area is a focus of oceanographic research for the University of Washington and the National Science Foundation’s Ocean Observatories Initiative, making it an ideal place to operate the project and monitor environmental conditions, Redd said.

From the vessel, Endurance guided down a modified geotechnical drill that offshore oil and gas developers typically use to extract core samples of subsea rocks. The team remotely drilled a relatively shallow well into a vent field at the base of the volcano, from which flowed hot, mineral-rich seawater.

Endurance then lowered Adélie onto the seafloor, where a submarine robot connected it to the well. The 3-ton power system contains an organic Rankine cycle system — the kind used on many land-based geothermal projects — that transfers heat from the hydrothermal fluid to spin a turbine and generate electricity.

Ultimately, Adélie wasn’t able to produce power from the well. So Endurance moved the unit to a nearby natural vent. On Sept. 27, the turbine produced about 60 watt-hours over about 29 seconds. For nearly 9 of those seconds, it generated more power than it used to operate, with the extra electricity charging the battery backup system. But the run ended after the battery’s overcurrent protection kicked in; when a power cable failed soon after, the dive was over.

“This was our first end-to-end demonstration of subsea geothermal as a concept, and we learned just an incredible amount from every stop along the way,” Redd said. A crew in Seattle received real-time temperature and flow-rate data from the site and operated the plant remotely using an existing fiber-optic cable network.

Endurance now is ​“rearchitecting” some of the core components of Adélie, he said. The startup plans to deploy the refurbished unit this winter with the aim of generating higher power output and for a longer stretch of time. At the same time, the company is developing what could become a far heftier commercial-scale system, which Redd posited might start generating electricity in 2027.

description:
Cyclones, storms, heatwaves, floods, and droughts continue to put critical infrastructure, homes, livelihoods, and lives at risk in the U.S. and around the world.

text:
Severe weather conditions have become constant. Cyclones, storms, heatwaves, floods, and droughts continue to put critical infrastructure, homes, livelihoods, and lives at risk in the U.S. and around the world.

Heat waves and droughts are the second-deadliest weather category, causing critical infrastructure instability, power line inefficiency, thermal sagging, and overloaded transformers that can lead to load shedding or automatically shut down critical systems. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recorded 2023 as “the fifth-warmest year in the 129-year record for the country as a whole.”

COMMENTARY

Nationwide, heat waves turning into heat domes are becoming annual occurrences as the frequency of high-temperature days and peak heat conditions rise year over year.

Monitoring Solutions for Critical Infrastructure Operations

According to the N1Critical stats, interrupted operations at healthcare facilities cost more than “$600,000 per hour ($7,500/minute) with delayed care, emergency diversions ($8,000–$13,000/hour), and lost surgical volume.” Interruptions in manufacturing facilities can cost an average of about $260,000 per hour with “halting production lines and idle labor.” In data centers, downtime costs range between “$300,000 to $540,000 per hour ($9,000/minute), driven by customer churn, data recovery, and SLA penalties.”

To maintain uninterrupted operations, critical infrastructure organizations need solutions that can provide proactive monitoring and alerting of all key components in mechanical and electrical systems. Continuous monitoring provides engineers and operators with real-time views of equipment and systems and ensures optimal operations regardless of outdoor conditions.

IIoT and SCADA platforms enable teams to monitor and analyze data from different sources over time with real-time alerts and actionable insights that expedite tactical equipment repairs without on-site manual equipment and systems inspection. Live data reports also help detect and address deviations from standard conditions before equipment failures. This allows engineers and operators to proactively deploy resources as needed to prevent downtime.

Extreme Heat Jeopardizes Grid Stability

Extreme heat not only drives electricity demand to record highs; it also dramatically strains all aspects of the grid. Surging temperatures affect the entire infrastructure ecosystem, starting from power generation plants and extending to local distribution lines.

When grids are strained, demands increase, and systems’ efficiencies drop as grid operators face near-record loads. With air conditioners, electric vehicles (EVs), and other energy-intensive systems operating continuously in both residential and commercial settings, electricity consumption surges, increasing demands on the power grid. Extended high temperatures also decrease the efficiency of transmission lines, transformers, and substations, which need higher energy levels to power in-house temperature-sensitive industrial cooling systems.

This past July, an hourly peak load in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the regional transmission organization serving most of Texas, broke a record of 91.1 gigawatts (GW), according to data reported by Hourly Electric Grid Monitor. The PJM Interconnection, the grid serving 67 million customers in 13 mid-Atlantic states, reported that power demand hit 162 GW around 6 p.m. on July 2 — the second-highest level ever recorded by PJM.

To avoid blackouts, local utilities and cooperatives nationwide issue public alerts requesting their utility customers to stop using major appliances and conserve electricity during peak afternoon and evening hours. Commercial consumers are requested and, in some cases, mandated to shed load during peak periods. The U.S. Department of Energy has authorized emergency orders that allow grid operators to direct large energy users like data centers to switch to backup generation supplies before declaring severe emergency alerts.

Preemptive Safeguards of Critical Infrastructure

With frequent, longer-lasting heat waves, organizations must consider comprehensive monitoring systems that can integrate seamlessly across portfolio sites, existing systems, and devices. To avoid costly consequences, operators can be preemptive with preventive maintenance of legacy and new equipment, systems, and devices to eliminate major failures and costly shutdowns.

A failure in the cooling system can cause equipment to overheat, resulting in a controlled shutdown to prevent complete equipment failure. When equipment goes down, services to end-users at data centers, telecom towers, utility distribution centers, and other locations will lag, interrupting or delaying automated and digitized services like banking, fueling your vehicle, internet searches, or using electrical appliances.

Ongoing heat waves also cause load increases in operational systems. Without constant monitoring of operating parameters and fault indicators, operators risk more frequent maintenance and higher costs. Operating systems at higher loads may seem like a good short-term solution, but it increases energy consumption and, in the long run, causes premature failure of system components, drastically raising operating costs.

Organizations with new mechanical systems should consider a redesign to optimize operational efficiency in higher ambient temperatures. Operators must closely monitor newly installed high-efficiency mechanical systems and existing HVAC and cooling configurations, which can’t handle rising ambient temperatures without a complete redesign.

Rising temperatures decrease the efficiency of air-cooled condensers. And since newer systems operate with tighter tolerances, their performance can drop more rapidly with increasing ambient temperature limits. To prevent thermal overload, modern equipment needs adjusted refrigerant charges and precise airflow. Upgrading fans and ductwork can improve higher air volumes and heat rejection capability.

Engineers designing systems must consider their equipment limitations relative to overall system capabilities. To avoid system failures during extreme weather conditions, engineers should:

Use regionally updated weather data when calculating their cooling loads. Historical weather averages are unreliable as conditions shift drastically.

Choose units with wider coil surface areas for ambient operations to help upsize condenser capacity to meet rising heat waves.

Better ventilation, in mechanical rooms or rooftop airflow, can release trapped heat that accumulates around equipment.

Optimize controls by using smart staging controls to manage compressors with multi-stage or variable speeds.

Drastic weather conditions are becoming common. Protecting critical infrastructure during such periods can be managed with real-time data monitoring solutions that track all connected equipment and systems and allow preemptive measures to ensure uninterrupted operations.

text:
In a new sign that U.S. electric utilities could eventually embrace small modular reactor nuclear technologies, American Electric Power (AEP) announced it will partner with SMR developer X-energy and Amazon to examine the feasibility of next-gen nuclear power in Indiana.

The joint development agreement between AEP and X-energy is focused on potentially building a 960-MW advanced nuclear power plant at a former coal-fired generation site in Sullivan County. Amazon is connected as a supporter through a funding agreement.

“Advanced nuclear energy has the potential to provide dependable power for over half a century while supporting economic growth in our communities. With this development plan, we are working to bring together the resources to help meet unprecedented growth in energy demand with reliable baseload power while protecting affordability for existing customers," AEP CEO and President Bill Fehrman said in a statement. “Our agreements with Amazon and X-energy will provide all necessary capital protections and financial safeguards that we have said are essential for any potential nuclear project to move forward.”

If a positive final investment decision is reached, building the Sullivan County project would generate baseload, carbon-free electricity through X-energy’s Xe-100 SMR technology. The initial project could include up to 12 Xe-100 units generating 80 MW each of SMR capacity.

In a separate deal, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is currently evaluating permitting the X-energy SMR to power chemical firm Dow’s Seadrift manufacturing site in Texas. The NRC could approve the Seadrift SMR project’s construction permit by the end of this year, according to reports.

If approved, the AEP and X-energy collaboration could build an SMR plant operational by early next decade at the former Indiana Michigan Power (I&M) coal-fired Breed Generation Station in Sullivan County. I&M is an AEP subsidiary utility, and Sullivan County recently joined the Indiana Advanced Nuclear Ready Communities Program.

“Indiana is building an energy future that prioritizes affordability for Hoosier families and businesses while driving economic growth,” Indiana Gov. Mike Braun said in the AEP release. “The decision by I&M/AEP, Amazon and X-energy to explore this technology in one of Indiana’s counties represents the kind of innovation and investment that can deliver lasting benefits for our state.”

In November 2025, Amazon announced it planned to invest $15 billion to add 2.4 GW of new data center campuses in northern Indiana. Overall, Amazon has spent or announced more than $30 billion on Indiana facilities.

“This collaboration with AEP and X-energy would enable us to make progress on both while ensuring that Indiana’s communities benefit,” Josh Weissman, vice president of data center infrastructure capacity delivery at Amazon, said in a statement. “Together, we’re looking to develop nearly a gigawatt of carbon-free power for the regional grid and pay our full costs without passing them to others. This project would also create jobs and generate tax revenues to benefit Hoosier communities for decades to come.”

The SMR movement has gained the support of President Trump’s administration through the U.S. Department of Energy and its pilot programs. Mostly, however, it’s been private ventures and investments from hyperscalers that are funding the future of small and next-gen reactor technologies.

The list of utilities working on SMR agreements is small, although larger utility holding companies such as Constellation are working with hyperscalers to reopen or keep existing nuclear power plants open. One of those deals includes Amazon's power purchase agreement with Constellation to expand the Calvert Cliffs nuclear power station in Maryland.

text:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas —

When you open your ballot, you'll see Proposition B, which begins by asking whether "Article IX for the city charter be amended to terminate and prohibit programs that exempt large industrial water users from drought surcharges."

Behind all those big words is a simpler way to describe Prop B.

Proposition B, otherwise known as the "Fair Water Amendment."

Breaking down Corpus Christi's Proposition B, the 'Fair Water Amendment'

It's an amendment to the city charter that would eliminate a "drought surcharge exemption fee" for large volume water users.

In a drought, if a regular person, a small business like a restaurant, or a refinery uses more water than they are allowed, they could be subject to paying extra for overusing the water.

Industrial water users like the refineries pay 31 cents extra for every 1,000 gallons of water they use. Paying that keeps them from having to pay the potential fees that would come in a drought.

Chloe Torres, the Coastal Bend regional coordinator for the Texas Campaign for the Environment, is one of the people who worked to secure over 12,000 verified signatures to add this to the ballot.

"Prop B is fundamentally about making sure that all water customers are paying into the same rules, playing by the same rules," she said.

Roland Barrera, a Corpus Christi City Council member at-large, sees it differently.

"You have these organizations that are outside Corpus Christi that are basically trying to stop the growth of industry. What they've done is created this initiative with local activists that have put this referendum against our economy and industry," Barrera said.

Torres and Barrera, despite their difference of opinion, both agree that industrial customers use more water than residents do.

"How much more of a financial burden are we going to place on residents when we're not the main users of water?" Torres said.

But Barrera argued the measure does little to protect residents.

"I don't think it has anything to do with basically providing water for residential ratepayers because their water was always preserved. If the majority of our water goes to industry then we have to cut back... then the majority of cutback is going to be from those individuals," Barrera said.
