WATKINS, Colo. — One of Colorado’s largest solar farms is coming to Adams County.

On Oct. 13, the county’s board of commissioners approved 2,800 acres in Watkins for the project, allowing Lightsource bp, a leading solar developer owned by British oil and gas giant BP, to use the land for the solar facility for the next 40 years.

The $675 million project, named Big Bronco Solar and Storage, will sit just east of Denver International Airport. It will include an 1,800-acre solar farm, a utility substation, a transmission line and a battery storage system.

“Power from this project can easily flow into Denver, where most of Xcel's load is, without the need for Xcel to build costly new transmission or make costly transmission upgrades,” said Will Vaughan, a development manager for Renewables at Lightsource bp. “So this contributes to keeping everybody’s power prices lower.”

The solar farm is expected to generate 300 megawatts of electricity — enough to power about 99,000 homes, according to the company. The battery system will store excess energy for later use and can deliver up to 300 megawatts of power.

A 2026 report released by Lazard finds that renewables remain the cheapest sources of new power generation, even without subsidies. Due to their relatively low costs and shorter construction times than natural gas, nuclear and coal plants, wind, solar and battery storage are expected to account for most new U.S. power sources in the coming years.

Colorado reflects this national trend. In 2025, wind, solar and geothermal sources supplied about 44% of the state’s electricity. By 2030, Colorado aims to increase that share to more than 80%.

Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to restrict the growth of renewable energy, the U.S. clean energy sector continues to boom. In 2025, wind and solar generated a record 17% of U.S. electricity. Wind power generation rose 3% from the previous year, while utility scale solar generation jumped 34%.

Some of the largest renewable energy projects, particularly wind, are concentrated in Colorado’s eastern plains. Kit Carson is home to eight wind farms and is becoming a giant hub for green energy, with two new projects under construction and a few more planned. The county generates 3.3 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity annually from wind power.

Other wind projects in the eastern plains include Limon Wind Energy Center, a 600-megawatt wind farm in Limon that stretches across 104,000 acres and came online in 2014. It can power about 114,000 homes. The Niyol Wind Energy Center in Logan County is a 200-megawatt wind farm that came online in 2021 and generates enough electricity to power approximately 60,000 homes.

Solar energy is also expanding across the region, with solar farms in Logan and Weld counties. Pueblo County in southern Colorado is a major solar hub, accounting for nearly half of the state’s solar farm acreage as of 2024.

Since 2010, the state has more than tripled renewable energy generation driven by the growth of wind farms on the Eastern Plains and solar installations across the state. Colorado became the fourth state to legalize small, plug-in solar systems, allowing residents to install up to four solar panels on balconies, patios and yards. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

The proposed Big Bronco Solar and Storage project would add to the state’s solar capacity. According to Lightsource bp, the project is expected to generate about $40 million in property tax revenue for Adams County special districts over its lifespan and employ up to 400 workers during peak construction, with many hired locally.

There was no local opposition to the project during public hearings.

Dennis Davis, who manages Davis Farm LLC, a 320-acre dryland farm north of the proposed site that has been in his family for five generations, said he supports the project.

“Farmers out there are at the whim of Mother Nature and Mother Nature’s been getting more and more cruel,” Davis said. “As a neighboring property, I feel it [the solar farm] would be a very positive use for the property.”

Adams County resident Charles Cipriani also voiced support for the project, but recommended a bond related to the decommissioning of the lithium iron phosphate cells of the batteries.

“It is not economically viable to recycle lithium iron phosphate cells and so someone will have to pay for it or it will not be done, so I would highly recommend that you have a bond in place,” Cipriani said at the public hearing. “It is environmentally exhaustive and unsafe to dispose of the batteries without property managing the recycling of them.”

Adams County planners with the community and economic development department said it is something they will follow up on.

A proposed 900-acre solar farm near Mesa Verde National Park is also facing scrutiny over battery storage. Some residents are concerned about the project’s size and the batteries’ proximity to the park and nearby communities, particularly following a January 2025 fire at a battery storage facility in Moss Landing, California. Though not a solar farm, the battery that caught fire stored electricity for later use.

Construction for Big Bronco Solar and Storage is not expected to begin for another two years and the company is still seeking a buyer for the electricity the project would generate.

Site management will also play a role in how the project is developed, the company outlined in their development plan. Because the land was a former dryland farming area, Lightsource bp plans to restore native vegetation, manage erosion and conserve topsoil to protect the site during all project phases.

​​Lightsource bp operates two other large-scale solar projects in Colorado, both in Pueblo County. The company reports conserving more than 3,000 acres of native shortgrass prairie across the two sites. Bighorn Solar, a 300-megawatt facility, began operating in 2021, followed by the 293-megawatt Sun Mountain Solar facility in 2022.

Currently ​​Lightsource bp has 33 projects operating across 11 states.

authors: Oliver Milman, Rachel Santarsiero, Jonathan Watts, Tim Murphy, Sara Sneath, Stephanie Mencimer, Alex Nguyen, Sophie Hurwitz, Jody Freeman, Jeff St. John

text:
This story was originally published by the Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Most Americans feel unease or alarm about the climate crisis and, in both red and blue states, want to know how political leaders are going to fix it. But in midterm election campaigns across the US, candidates have responded to this desire with near silence.

People in the US have this year endured a record hot summer as well as soaring costs, equating to roughly $2,000 per household, in extra energy and mortgage payments, due to the country’s dependence on a fossil fuel supply scrambled by Donald Trump’s decision to attack Iran.

Yet the unfolding climate crisis, and the imperative to transition to cleaner, less volatile forms of energy, has been starkly absent on campaign trails before the midterms in three weeks’ time. Even among previously pro-green Democrats, 2026 has seen a widespread climate omertà.

“Look, I’m not going to defend the Green New Deal,” Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Michigan, told Fox News in August, after previously campaigning for 100 percent renewable energy.

Jon Ossoff, seeking to retain his Senate seat in Georgia, has ditched mentions of the environment in favor of focusing on the Iran war and inflation. Meanwhile, James Talarico, another leading Democratic Senate hope who previously compared oil and gas to 1980s cassette tapes that are “not gonna last,” has struck a very different tone in this campaign.

“I support our oil and gas industry,” Talarico, aiming for a first Democratic win in Texas in decades, said last month. “I had family members who worked in the industry. I went to public schools here in Texas funded by the oil and gas industry.”

Among all Democratic and Republican candidates in eight battleground states that will determine control of the Senate—Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Iowa, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas—none mention “climate” on their campaign websites other than El-Sayed and Talarico.

This so-called “climate hushing,” however, is disconnected from what voters actually want, polling suggests. Three times as many voters in these eight swing states want politicians to spend more time talking about the climate crisis than those who want to hear less about it, a large survey from last month found, with thumping majorities in each state saying they are more likely to vote for a candidate who prioritizes a transition to clean energy.

“The climate hushers are dead wrong—voters want to hear more about climate change, not less, and they will reward politicians who are strong climate leaders,” said Nathaniel Stinnett, executive director of the Environmental Voter Project, which conducted the poll. “Politicians should always tailor their message to their district but it’s pure fiction to say that talking about climate change will lose you votes.”

“In fact, it’s a huge vote-winner, even with independents in red states who favor fairly aggressive climate action by a four-to-one margin,” Stinnett added. “There’s this idea that climate has become a curse word and you shouldn’t say it. That’s just wrong.”

Midterm candidates may have disparaged or ignored climate action in search of electability, but the data indicates a mainstream position among US voters is concern about climate change and support for a prompt switch away from fossil fuels. More Americans are starting to link their rising living costs with fossil fuels and climate-driven disasters, too, despite a dwindling interest in political and media circles to mention such connections.

“The norm has shifted, yet so many politicians seem stuck in a 1990s world where clean energy and climate change are radical, fringe things that only environmentalists think about,” said Anthony Leiserowitz, an expert in climate communication at Yale University.

“This climate-hushing strategy, which has been adopted by many politicians, is not a logical response to where voters are,” he added. Yale’s own polling has found a majority of Americans remain worried about global heating despite the electoral success of Donald Trump, who has called climate science “a hoax.”

This is the case even in major oil and gas producing states: in the Environmental Voter Project polling released last month, 54 percent of voters in Texas said they’d be more likely to vote for a pro-renewables candidate, compared with 19 percent who said they’d be less likely, with more Texans more favorable of solar and wind energy than oil.

Despite this, Republicans have sought to paint Talarico as an eco-extremist bent on shutting down the oil and gas industry, with Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued GOP candidate, calling his opponent “Tofu Talarico” and an enemy of the fossil fuel sector.

“In Texas, he talks about: ‘I’m a vaygan [sic], I’m a vaygan.’ He’s a vaygan meaning he likes lettuce,” Trump said about Talarico at a rally this month, with the president mis-pronouncing the word “vegan.” (Talarico is not a vegan.) “And now he goes to every barbecue available. He then throws up immediately after eating the steak. Throwing up all over the place.”

In Alaska, there is even stronger support for renewables, with 63 percent of voters saying they’d back a campaign that prioritizes the transition to clean energy. Mary Peltola, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Alaska who has run on a tagline of “fish, family, freedom,” has called for the return of tax credits for clean energy but also demands more oil be refined in the state and has pushed for the approval of a large oil project in the Alaskan Arctic.

“Increasing Alaska energy production is critical to addressing the affordability crisis, and Mary will aggressively advocate for every solution on the table—including increased oil and gas production, as well as restoring tax credits for solar, wind and hydropower projects that were cut by Dan Sullivan,” said a Peltola spokesperson, referencing her Republican opponent, who voted with other GOP lawmakers to gut Joe Biden-era legislation to boost renewables.

The Trump administration, which has moved to eliminate any limits on greenhouse gas pollution while bolstering the fossil fuel industry, considers the climate issue to be in full retreat. “You don’t hear the word ‘climate change’ as much as you did two years ago, because the legs have been knocked out from under that movement,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, claimed last week.

Media mentions of the climate crisis have dropped in the past year and the issue has slipped down the list of voters’ stated priorities as inflation has taken its toll and alarm over the Iran war and the state of US democracy has surged. Candidates faced with limited cash and fractured voter attention spans have found it expedient to focus on these headline topics, rather than global heating.

Attitudes towards the climate crisis also continue to differ sharply by party affiliation, with Democrats still overwhelmingly the most concerned about the issue and Republicans far more likely to see it as a trivial or even non-existent problem. This has spurred many Democrats running in states previously won by Trump to bury any mention of climate, although some have bucked this strategy.

“Voters are concerned about the climate. Sometimes people just don’t understand how it impacts the cost of things like insurance, which is unfortunate,” said Angie Nixon, a Democrat running a surprisingly competitive Senate race in Florida, which has become a Republican stronghold in recent years.

Nixon has, unlike most other candidates from both parties, repeatedly mentioned her state’s vulnerability to the climate crisis during her campaign. “A lot of Florida will be under water in the next few decades and I’m worried about that,” she said. “I want the world to be around for my kids. Young people really care about climate change because they know it will really affect them.”

Democrats have long had a “weak” message on the climate crisis because they simply repeat back to voters what polls tell them the most pressing issues are, the Democratic senator and climate advocate Sheldon Whitehouse has argued. His party should instead actively raise and weaponize the climate crisis, Whitehouse insists, much like how Republicans do for far more niche topics, such as trans people playing sports.

“This is a story with villains—the greedy fossil fuel companies wrecking the planet and sticking Americans with the bill for the damage,” Whitehouse said. “Frustrated voters are hungry to see politicians really fighting for them, and the climate fight presents a real opportunity to show them that we are.”

But for the growing cohort of Americans who have had their lives upended by extreme events such as storms, floods, and wildfires—by one estimate, this includes about a third of all people in the US over the previous two years—there is scant evidence of a fight being waged on their behalf to stem the rising temperatures that worsen such calamities.

At a meeting of disaster survivors in Kerrville, Texas, last week, several people who endured deadly flash floods that swept through the region last year—killing 136 people, including 28 of whom were at a riverside Christian camp for girls—expressed frustration that politicians have tuned out of their plight.

“I think that a lot of politicians couldn’t be bothered, they couldn’t be bothered by it,” said Georgia Bishop, an 18-year-old whose best friend, Felicity Jarmon, died in the floods. “They see it, they know it, they’ve heard us scream to the rooftops about it. But it just seems to be: ‘Well, this is weather, this is life.’”

A developing El Niño climate event, already one of the strongest ever recorded, is set to further accelerate extreme heat and flooding risk in parts of the US in the coming months. Bishop said at this point she wouldn’t be surprised to see a snowstorm in Texas in July. The political indifference to this is, she added, “infuriating.”

The Republican and Democratic Senate candidates from the key eight battleground states—Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Iowa, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas—were all contacted for comment about their stance, or lack of it, on the climate crisis.

text:
From application lab validation to integrated solution

ASSLAR, GERMANY, October 19, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Hydrogen components must function safely under demanding conditions. Tanks, lines, valves and other components are subjected to mechanical, thermal and pressure-related loads as part of validation and approval testing. Leak testing is a key part of these test sequences. It verifies whether a component remains reliably tight after defined load cycles.

Resato High Pressure Technology is headquartered in Assen, the Netherlands, and employs 65 people. The company develops and builds high-pressure solutions for a large variety of markets and application areas, including the hydrogen sector. These hydrogen systems are used to test and validate tanks, components and hoses under realistic conditions. The challenge is not only to generate and control high pressures safely. Leak testing also has to be integrated reliably into the overall process and deliver reproducible results.

For a hydrogen gas test system used to validate hydrogen storage vessels, Resato was looking for a suitable leak detection solution. The requirements were demanding: the measurement technology had to be integrated into a complex high-pressure test environment, deliver stable results over longer measurement periods and comply with the safety-related framework of the system.

Feasibility study in the application laboratory

In order to identify the most suitable leak detector for long-term qualification processes in the hydrogen economy, Resato turned to Pfeiffer Vacuum+Fab Solutions. The project began with a feasibility study in the Application Laboratory of Pfeiffer in Asslar, Germany. Using Resato’s own test and calibration setup, the teams carried out measurements, evaluated the behavior of the system and assessed how the leak detection technology could later be integrated into the Resato test system.

By evaluating the application under realistic operating conditions, Resato and Pfeiffer gained insights that could not be derived from technical specifications alone. The focus included long-term stability, background signal behavior, temperature influences and practical integration into the test setup.

The feasibility study created a reliable basis for selecting the final solution. Especially in safety-relevant hydrogen applications, this kind of preliminary validation reduces technical uncertainty and helps avoid incorrect investment decisions. At the same time, Pfeiffer was able to understand the customer’s requirements in detail to design the solution for the specific application.

Two tracer gas leak detectors in the test system

Following the evaluation, Resato selected two ASM 340 tracer gas leak detectors. They were integrated into Resato’s high-pressure test solution for hydrogen applications, including the testing of hydrogen tanks for the automotive sector as well as components for the transport and storage of pure hydrogen.

During the test sequence, the tank is conditioned, pressurized and then subjected to permeation and leak testing. Depending on the tank size and customer-specific requirements, different test conditions must be covered. The tanks are pressurized and tested in a pressure range from 350 to 875 bar (35 to 87.5 MPa).

For safety reasons, the ASM 340 leak detectors were installed in a separate, protected area outside the ATEX zone. This spatial separation protects the measurement technology from the explosion-hazard area while still allowing seamless integration into the automated test process. Each leak detector is fully integrated into the overall testing process and the Resato HMI for easy control and automated operation. Communication with the system is handled via an RS-232 interface. The permeation and leak testing runs automatically, and the measurement data is transferred directly into the final test report for the customer. The ASM leak detectors are calibrated using an external calibrated hydrogen leak. This supports reliable measurement results under the specific conditions of the application.

Standards such as R134 and UN GTR No. 13-2 define the regulatory framework. Implementing these requirements in a reliable test system calls for the combined technical expertise of Resato and Pfeiffer: Resato provides the high-pressure system, test chambers and safety technology, while Pfeiffer contributes the leak detection technology and application-specific measurement support.

Integrated leak testing for demanding hydrogen applications

The decisive factor was the close cooperation between both parties in developing a solution that had not previously existed in this form. The application required more than selecting a suitable leak detector: leak testing had to become a reliable part of a high-pressure test, with demanding requirements for safety, automation and measurement stability. Through ongoing feasibility testing, Pfeiffer helped establish a reliable basis for the industrial solution and supported the final decision-making process.

Today, ASM 340 leak detectors support leak testing within the Resato test system. The detectors enable stable measurements over longer periods and can be safely integrated into the test sequence.

Support also continued after the sale. Resato received further assistance with measurement-related questions and the evaluation of test results, including how parameters such as temperature can affect leak-rate measurements. This is particularly important because measurement values in complex test systems must always be assessed in the context of the setup, environmental conditions, and test parameters.

“The cooperation with Pfeiffer Vacuum+Fab Solutions helped us identify the right solution for our application”, says Stefan Langeland, Mechanical Engineer at Resato. ”The combination of measurement technology, application expertise and continuous support was key to successfully integrating leak testing into our test system. This has led to an unprecedented method of testing and validating objects using pure hydrogen.”

A transferable concept for the hydrogen sector

The project shows that reliable leak testing in the hydrogen sector requires more than suitable equipment. Especially in approval and qualification testing, measurement technology must be understood in the context of the full test setup, environmental conditions and applicable test requirements. Otherwise, repeated testing can lead to additional costs, longer approval processes and delayed time to market.

An early feasibility study helps reduce this risk. It creates confidence before investment, makes technical interdependencies visible and supports the safe integration of leak testing into demanding hydrogen test systems. This applies not only to tank testing, but also to hose testing and component testing where high pressure, gas permeation and leak testing come together to meet testing requirements. For test system manufacturers, test laboratories and companies in the hydrogen sector, this provides a transferable concept for future applications: robust measurement technology, process understanding and application support combined in one reliable and efficient testing solution.

Europe illustrates the policy effect, with sales increasing more than 30% following the implementation of stricter EU CO2 standards. This suggests that future market expansion will depend not only on incentives but also on manufacturers' ability to offer cost-competitive EVs across mainstream vehicle segments.

BEV Growth Is Being Driven by Decreasing Battery Cost and Increasing Charging Performance and Powertrain Efficiency

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), LFP batteries accounted for more than 55% of global EV battery deployment in 2025, up from nearly 50% in 2024. The increasing adoption of LFP is supported by its lower material costs and reduced dependence on nickel and cobalt, making the chemistry increasingly important for cost-competitive mass-market BEVs. Charging performance is also becoming a competitive differentiator, reducing the need for oversized battery packs to deliver practical driving range. In March 2026, BYD introduced its second-generation Blade Battery with FLASH Charging, supporting 10% to 97% charging in 9 minutes at up to 1,500 kW, alongside plans for 20,000 FLASH charging stations in China by the end of 2026. Battery technology is also moving toward higher energy density and faster charging, with CATL unveiling in April 2026 a next-generation battery supporting a 1,000 km range and a Shenxing battery capable of charging from 10% to 98% in under seven minutes. BEV growth is increasingly being supported by lower battery costs, higher energy density, faster charging, and improved powertrain efficiency, allowing OEMs to improve vehicle usability without relying solely on larger battery capacities.

Passenger Cars Remain the Core EV Segment as Platform Economics and Technology Improve

The passenger car segment is expected to retain the largest share of the electric vehicle market, supported by the increasing economic and technical competitiveness of EV platforms. Battery cost, charging speed, vehicle efficiency, and platform scalability are becoming the main factors influencing OEM investment and product deployment. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electric car sales exceeded 20 million units in 2025, representing 25% of new car sales, while BEVs increased their share of electric car sales to 65%. The technology focus is shifting toward higher energy density, faster charging, lower vehicle weight, and more efficient electric powertrains, allowing OEMs to improve range without continuously increasing battery capacity. BMW's 2026 Neue Klasse platform illustrates this transition, with its sixth-generation eDrive technology using an 800-volt architecture, cell-to-pack battery integration, and cylindrical cells with 20% higher cell-level energy density. The BMW iX3 can add up to 372 km of range in 10 minutes at a 400 kW charger, while the new BMW i3 is designed for up to 900 km of range and 400 km of added range in 10 minutes.

Ultra-fast charging is also becoming a vehicle platform differentiator. In March 2026, BYD introduced its second-generation Blade Battery and FLASH Charging system, supporting charging power of up to 1,500 kW, with a 10% to 97% charge in nine minutes. BYD also planned 20,000 FLASH charging stations in China by the end of 2026, linking vehicle battery capability with dedicated high-power charging infrastructure. The regulatory environment is reinforcing passenger car electrification, particularly in Europe. The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) reported that BEVs reached 20.7% of EU new car registrations in H1 2026, compared with 15.6% in H1 2025, with France, Germany, and Denmark recording strong increases. ACEA attributed the broader electrified vehicle market partly to new and revised tax benefits and incentive schemes. The IEA also identifies CO2 and fuel economy standards as the main driver of EV sales growth outside China, while competitive EV economics are already supporting adoption in China and some emerging markets.

China is set to be the largest market in Asia Pacific during the forecast period.

China is expected to remain the largest electric vehicle market in Asia Pacific, with future revenue opportunities extending beyond vehicle sales into batteries, ultra-fast charging, intelligent driving, battery swapping, and commercial fleet electrification. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports that electric cars represented nearly 55% of Chinese car sales in 2025, while China produced nearly 75% of global electric cars and more than 80% of global battery cells. In 2025, around 70% of BEVs sold in China were already cheaper than the average conventional car, showing that EV adoption is increasingly supported by vehicle economics. Passenger SUVs and medium-sized BEVs provide substantial vehicle revenue opportunities, while electric heavy trucks offer a high-utilization commercial opportunity supported by operating cost advantages. Meanwhile, China's scale in battery manufacturing, charging infrastructure, and intelligent vehicle technology is creating adjacent revenue pools in battery services, charging networks, power electronics, ADAS software, and vehicle technology licensing. This makes China an important market not only for EV manufacturers but also for suppliers across the wider EV technology and energy ecosystem. Investment Funding Context

Investment activity in the electric vehicle market increased during 2024 to 2026, with capital increasingly moving beyond vehicle development toward battery manufacturing, localized EV production, software, critical minerals, and regional supply chains. CATL also raised USD 5 billion through a Hong Kong share offering to support global factory expansion and R&D. In 2025, Volkswagen invested another USD 1 billion in Rivian as part of its EV software and electrical architecture partnership, while Tata Group continued its approximately USD 1.5 billion investment in its Agratas battery manufacturing project in India. In 2024, major commitments included Hyundai Motor Group's USD 51 billion three-year investment program in South Korea focused on EV production and new mobility, Toyota's USD 1.4 billion investment in its Indiana EV facility, and Volkswagen's initial USD 2.3 billion investment in Rivian and its EV software joint venture. These investments indicate a shift from establishing basic EV production capacity toward integrated EV ecosystems combining vehicle manufacturing, battery production, software, charging, and critical material supply chains, with companies increasingly localizing production to strengthen cost competitiveness and regional supply security.

Revenue Shift Context

EV revenue is moving from a predominantly transactional model toward a lifecycle and recurring revenue model. Vehicle sales and batteries will continue to form the core revenue base because EV adoption itself is expanding. However, the installed vehicle base creates additional monetization opportunities after the initial sale, particularly through software, charging, energy management, battery lifecycle services, fleet platforms, and autonomous mobility. This shift is supported by the expected scale of EV deployment. The IEA projects that the global EV fleet, excluding electric two- and three-wheelers, will exceed 450 million vehicles by 2035 under current policies, more than five times the fleet at the end of 2025. The larger installed base provides the foundation for recurring revenue streams that were relatively small during the early EV market.

Mergers and Acquisitions

From 2025 to 2026, approximately 12-15 notable M&A transactions and acquisitions involving electric vehicle market companies or dedicated electric vehicle capabilities were identified, although most did not disclose transaction values.

Like the head-turning Roadster it reintroduced last week with some snazzy new performance features, Tesla(NASDAQ: TSLA) shares come with a big price tag. The stock enters this week at $354.72.

Despite the triple-digit price of admission, now could be a good time to buy at least a single share. Even if your broker is open to selling you fractional shares, going with a round share is more than just a cleaner transaction. It provides you with full voting power and the ability to transfer to a brokerage account, which may not allow fractional purchases.

It can fly

There's a lot going for Tesla stock these days. A surge in gas prices is boosting the value proposition of electric vehicles, reversing the bearish narrative that began for U.S. drivers in the fall of last year after federal tax credits of up to $7,500 for new purchases or leases expired.

The high-end Roadster is just one of the many new offerings coming from the world's most valuable automaker by market cap. Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots, improvements in its autonomous driving platform, and a push into commercial vehicles leave analysts expecting annual revenue to nearly double in the next three years.

Sticking the landing

A lot can also go wrong. Profitability was cut in half in its previous quarter. Analysts see a much smaller decline on the bottom line when it reports third-quarter results later this week, but it still needs to turn that around.

The top line has recovered quickly from last year's fourth-quarter decline, bringing us to today's opportunity. The shares are down 21% this year. The fundamentals are holding up better. Even as we head into Wednesday afternoon's financial update, analysts are bracing for flat sales. This is actually a good thing, since last year's third quarter was when sales spiked as U.S. buyers scrambled to get their orders in before the federal tax credit expired.

Tesla is out of favor with investors this year. Volatility has always been part of this story, but historically, as with its new Roadster Rocket, it's just a matter of time before it lifts off the ground.

It’s Monday, and that’s when we like to take a look at current business issues that are trending across our state and discuss them with one of our fellow news media friends. This week, Mike Switzer interviews Alan Cooper, founder and editor of three online business news websites in South Carolina: MidlandsBiz, UpstateBizSC, and LowCountryBizSC. TRANSCRIPT:

Switzer: Hello and welcome to another edition of the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer. It's Monday, and that's when we like to take a look at current business issues that are trending across our state and discuss them with one of our fellow news media friends. This week we have Alan Cooper, founder and editor of three online business news websites in South Carolina, Midlands Biz, Upstate Biz SC and Lowcountry Biz sc. Alan, welcome back to the program, Mike.

Cooper: Thanks for having me.

Switzer: So tell us what's showing up on your radar this week?

Cooper: What's showing up on my radar is what I'd like to position as, potentially one of the biggest economic opportunities that South Carolina could see over the next 50 years. I did an interview with a gentleman, works for a company called Dominion Engineering. It has nothing to do with Dominion Energy. This is a consulting firm that is helping businesses build new nuclear power plants. We've been talking about this nuclear resurgence. There's just been a complete shift in people's minds about nuclear power. We know that we need power to fuel all these data centers and the new manufacturing coming to the state and more people coming here. There's a huge demand for energy and the shift has happened in people's mindset about nuclear. Whereas before be hard pressed to find a community that would like to have a nuclear power plant, now states are kind of very open to this. Mike, here's what he was mentioning. Over the next 50 years or so, the projection is that there will be hundreds of new power plants built around the world. So some of the projections are in the 300, 400 or 500 new nuclear power plants. And I think the question is, Mike, is South Carolina in a position to capitalize and take on some of this new business as huge opportunity in, the nuclear industry?

Switzer: Well, well, I think so, because actually, I think we might have talked to the same person, Craig Stover, senior director for new nuclear deployment at Dominion Engineering. That's who you talked to? Yes, yes. And so I interviewed him back in May, and, he brought to our attention that the American Nuclear Society recently named our state third in the nation for nuclear power production. So, he seemed to believe, and his company believes, that that puts us in a pretty good position for nuclear energy growth.

Cooper: Yeah. And he does mention a couple of other things about the assets that we already have. So half of our nuclear, half of our power here in the state is generated already through nuclear power. We already have Westinghouse, who's been here for, decades, producing the fuel that goes into nuclear power plants. And Mike, just at the end of September, are we positioning ourselves to capitalize on this business? Well, what one of the key components is going to be the workforce. And what we saw come out of the the nuclear Power summit at the end of September was a partnership between the University of South Carolina School of Engineering and Westinghouse to, to combine to train, get South Carolina prepared for all the opportunities that are going to come in terms of workforce, in this new industry. So that's a key component of it is the workforce.

Switzer: Well you know, Westinghouse almost went under because of that SCANA, fiasco with that nuclear plant in Jenkinsville, that had to close. But yeah, so I mean it's looking good with the energy situation across the globe right now. Nuclear energy is looking pretty good.

Cooper: Yeah. So the, the other part of it is trying to out compete other states because we're not going to be the only state that is wants to capitalize on this business. So there's already nuclear power summits going on in other states, in Texas, in Tennessee, all over the country. Other states are aggressively going after competing for this nuclear investments. So what is South Carolina doing to support this? That's one of the questions that we need to ask and how can we also communicate this opportunity to supporting businesses, businesses that are currently here, manufacturers that could shift some of their production into the construction of these new nuclear facilities. there's just an amazing opportunity and as Craig said, he really feels like this is a once in a generation opportunity for South Carolina. So we just need to put all these pieces in place so that we can capitalize on it.

Switzer: Sounds good to me Alan. Thank you so much for your time today.

Cooper: Mike, thanks.

Switzer: Alan Cooper is founder and editor of three online business news websites in our state. We will have links to all of those posted at our webpage so you can learn more SouthCarolinaPublicRadio.org where you can hear this show again, and you can find us wherever you find podcasts. With the South Carolina Business Review, this is Mike Switzer.

text:
NEW ORLEANS — Renewable energy emerged as a recurring theme at Tulane University’s Future of Energy Forum, held Sept. 28–30 in New Orleans, as Louisiana confronts unprecedented electricity demand driven by a surge in industrial investment and data center development.

The forum drew more than 2,000 attendees to examine the state’s growing energy needs and the technologies and investments required to meet them. Louisiana Economic Development reported more than $183 billion in announced capital investment in 2026 as of Sept. 10, including major data center projects planned by Meta, Amazon and Hut 8.

“What was more interesting to me was how often renewable energy entered conversations that were not specifically about renewables,” said Jeff Arnold, Director of Powering Louisiana an initiative of the Southern Renewable Energy Association (SREA).

Arnold attributed the growing interest to two economic pressures: major industrial investors’ sustainability goals and the need to bring additional electricity generation online quickly. Utility-scale solar, he said, can be developed faster than some conventional power plants.

“That is important because this conversation is increasingly being driven by economics rather than politics,” Arnold wrote in an Oct. 5 commentary about the forum.

Renewable Energy Opportunities and Setbacks

Although oil and natural gas have historically dominated the nation’s energy industry, renewables and battery storage account for most new utility-scale generating and storage capacity planned for 2026. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, developers expect to add a record 86 gigawatts, with solar accounting for 51%, battery storage 28% and wind 14%, compared with approximately 7% for natural gas.

Despite uncertainty surrounding offshore wind development, Louisiana businesses could still benefit from projects elsewhere in the country. State Rep. Joseph Orgeron said at the Tulane forum that Louisiana shipyards could build specialized vessels, manufacturers could produce components, and marine service companies and ports could support offshore construction.

“In short, Louisiana’s offshore oil and gas industry didn’t leave us unprepared for the next generation of offshore energy. It helped build the workforce and infrastructure to compete,” Arnold wrote.

Federal Policy Complicates Renewable Energy Expansion

The Trump administration’s changes to federal energy and environmental policies are creating additional uncertainty for renewable developers, including those pursuing offshore wind projects.

In August, the administration canceled an offshore wind lease south of Lake Charles held by German energy company RWE as part of a $1.22 billion settlement covering the company’s leases in Louisiana, New York and California. RWE said it had invested more than $1 billion in its U.S. offshore wind leases and related development before concluding the projects could not obtain permits in the foreseeable future.

The settlement illustrates how federal energy policy can influence investment decisions. Following the agreement to relinquish its offshore wind leases, RWE announced $1.2 billion in natural gas-related investments, including $900 million for an indirect 16% stake in the Louisiana LNG project and a separate $300 million agreement to reserve turbines for future U.S. power generation projects.

The agreement has also prompted opposition from California officials. On Sept. 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Energy Commission issued a notice of intent to sue the U.S. Department of the Interior and RWE, alleging that the $1.22 billion settlement improperly uses federal taxpayer funds to cancel offshore wind leases and redirect investment toward fossil fuel projects. California argues that the agreement violates federal offshore leasing law and threatens investments in ports, manufacturing and jobs tied to offshore wind development.

Federal policy changes have also extended to emissions regulations. On Sept. 14, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized the repeal of most of the Biden administration’s 2024 greenhouse gas emission standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants and proposed eliminating the remaining requirements. The EPA estimates the finalized rollback will save approximately $310 billion, while opponents warn it could increase emissions and associated health risks. A coalition of states and local governments sued the EPA on Oct. 1.

Development Challenges in Louisiana

Renewable energy projects in Louisiana also face obstacles getting connected to the electricity grid. The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), which oversees the regional power grid, has a backlog of proposed projects awaiting studies and approvals needed to connect to the system. Those delays can slow development even when companies are ready to build new generating facilities.

Solar development has also encountered local opposition. In August, the Vernon Parish Police Jury approved a temporary moratorium on solar farm development in unincorporated areas of the parish, following residents’ concerns about a proposed large-scale project. Separately, a Louisiana law enacted in 2025 requires solar facilities covering 75 acres or more to obtain state permits and meet siting requirements, adding another layer of regulatory review for developers.

Grid connection delays and a changing permitting landscape can complicate investment decisions.

“Investors can price risk, but they struggle to price uncertainty,” Arnold wrote. “When the rules change after millions have been spent, the impact doesn’t stop at a single project—it influences future investment decisions.”

Conventional power generation faces its own delays. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission member David LaCerte said at the Tulane forum that natural gas turbine equipment backlogs stretch for years. For Arnold, this reinforces the potential value of developing solar and other resources while conventional plants are being built.

“If one resource takes years longer to deploy, then we should be developing other resources while it is being built,” Arnold said.

Grid Planning and Public Participation

A white paper released Oct. 12 by Powering Louisiana, the Southeastern Wind Coalition, Greater New Orleans Inc. and the Kathleen Babineaux Blanco Public Policy Center at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette identified electricity affordability, grid reliability and economic growth as interconnected challenges.

The report warned that heavy reliance on natural gas could expose customers to fuel-price volatility.

“Louisiana’s competitiveness depends on scaling sustainable fuels, decarbonizing our industries, and bringing reliable clean power online,” said Salem Habte, director of business development and innovation at Greater New Orleans Inc.

The report also emphasized treating the grid as economic infrastructure, particularly as industrial companies increasingly consider electricity availability when selecting locations.

“Wind energy, in combination with natural gas, nuclear, solar, and other technologies, can create a resilient energy grid that maximizes the benefits and minimizes the risks of each of these technologies,” said Madelyn Smith, senior program manager at the Southeastern Wind Coalition. “Our systems are strongest when we have a diversity of options available at any given moment.”

Arnold argued that developers should engage landowners, residents and local officials early.

“Developers need to know the rules. Communities deserve to know what is being proposed. Landowners deserve to understand how a project may affect their property. And elected officials need accurate information early enough in the process to make informed decisions,” he said. “Community engagement cannot begin at the public hearing.”

text:
Former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper's (D.) top climate advisers were paid for by a progressive nonprofit—the United Nations Foundation—in an initiative designed to enact left-wing climate policies at the state level, thus bypassing President Donald Trump's decision to withdraw America from the Paris Climate Accords, according to documents reviewed by the Washington Free Beacon. The advisers oversaw Cooper's policies prioritizing offshore wind projects, "decarbonizing" the state's electric grid, implementing electric car mandates, and making the state's buildings less dependent on natural gas.

Cooper's progressive environmental policies were deeply divisive in North Carolina, which leans conservative, but the state legislature's Republican supermajority ultimately blocked much of the Cooper administration's efforts. Cooper is now running for Senate, and polls show him with a strong lead over the Republican contender, Michael Whatley.

The Free Beacon obtained a trove of internal state documents showing that, beginning in 2020, Cooper's office submitted several applications for UNF grants worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to fund salary, benefits, and travel for its top climate policy staff. The UNF—a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit, founded by Ted Turner, that draws upon its more than $210 million endowment to directly support U.N. social and environmental activities—ultimately approved those requests and, between 2020 and 2024, awarded grants worth $1.7 million to the state, according to funding agreements and tax filings. That's more than any other state received under the initiative.

The advisers funded by the UNF grants were official North Carolina state employees.

The grants are part of the U.S. Climate Alliance initiative, which is housed at the UNF for what it says are "legal and fiduciary purposes" and was founded by a coalition of Democratic governors in June 2017 after Trump's decision to pull out of the Paris Accords. At the time, the founders, then-Govs. Jerry Brown (Calif.), Jay Inslee (Wash.), and Andrew Cuomo (N.Y.), said the alliance would uphold the accords' aggressive climate objectives via state-level policy. Cooper entered North Carolina into the initiative three months later, though his office never publicly disclosed that the UNF would be paying for his staff. Cooper's office privately requested that other states involved in the alliance not make "too big a deal" of the participation of North Carolina, whose voters are far more conservative than those in California, Washington, and New York.

The documents provide a window into how Cooper pursued some of the nation's most extreme climate policies, modeled his environmental agenda after California's, and did it all with the direct assistance of an outside progressive organization funded by liberal billionaire environmentalists like Turner, who died in May, and Bill Gates.

They also offer behind-the-scenes insight into the views of Cooper, who is again portraying himself as a moderate as he seeks a Senate seat. During this campaign, he has shied away from his climate record (his campaign website is devoid of any mention of climate change) and has instead broadly emphasized the importance of making energy more affordable, something critics say his climate policies failed to do.

"These policies that North Carolina put in place under Cooper would not do anything for the climate. We are simply too small of a state," Jon Sanders, the director of the North Carolina-based John Locke Foundation's energy center, said in an interview. "These policies can place significant costs on people in North Carolina that won't be faced by anybody else in the world. We can certainly make life a lot more difficult for North Carolinians in pursuit of this impossible goal."

Sanders added that it is "shocking and offensive" that Cooper pursued his policies with outside financial support from the UNF.

For Cooper, receiving outside funding to pursue left-wing climate initiatives was useful, as the legislature has made a practice of going through budgets with a scalpel and excising funding for staff and groups that pursued liberal policies on the taxpayer's dime.

North Carolina was among a handful of select states that the UNF's U.S. Climate Alliance consulted as it developed its "fellows program," the records obtained by the Free Beacon show. In an email sent in March 2019, the group's then-executive director Julie Cerqueira told a top official in Cooper's office that the goal would be to "help our states hire an additional staff person to support their policy priorities" and that she needed assistance crafting the program before she met with prospective donors. Tax filings show that the left-wing grantmakers the Sequoia Climate Fund, the William & Flora Hewlett Foundation, and the Rockefeller Brothers Fund were among the donors who eventually helped stand the program up.

Several months later, Cooper's office submitted an application for funding under the nascent program, which the UNF quickly approved. According to the agreement reviewed by the Free Beacon, the grant was worth $292,677 and funded the two-year salary of a new senior climate policy adviser who would be Cooper's highest-ranking staffer overseeing climate policy.

The application stated that the adviser would oversee implementation of Cooper's plans to push electric vehicles, develop a "strategic plan for eliminating greenhouse gas emissions from the transportation sector," and enter the state into new multi-state agreements on EVs. It added that they would be tasked with developing new actions to curb emissions from sources not yet regulated, like home appliances; representing the state and Cooper at climate conferences; and leading North Carolina's "efforts to advance offshore wind."

And the application added that a broad goal of the funding would be to ensure North Carolina's climate policy has a "ripple effect throughout the country."

"Many non-Alliance states consider themselves more like North Carolina than states on the West Coast or in the Northeast," it continued. "This is in part because North Carolina is a moderate state with divided government, one of only two southern states in the Alliance, and has a diverse geography. Non-Alliance states, especially those in the Southeast, look to North Carolina as a source of successful policies to replicate."

One year later, Cooper's office solicited another grant, this time worth $264,765 for the two-year salary of a second adviser who would serve as the first UNF-funded adviser's top deputy. The UNF again approved the request and provided the funding in April 2021.

In addition to assisting the senior adviser and allowing them to focus more on crafting new climate goals and executive orders, according to the application, the new staffer would "focus primarily on climate issues related to the transportation sectоr, government fleet conversion to zero-emission vehicles, building and energy efficiency, and industrial emissions."

As the point person on electric vehicle adoption, the new adviser would oversee a plan mandating the state government's fleet of vehicles be converted to electric and help evaluate whether North Carolina should enter the so-called Transportation Climate Initiative, a multi-state program led by Massachusetts to force emissions reductions and a transition to EVs. The new adviser would be tasked also with coordinating "climate justice" policies to make sure "environmental equity" was prioritized.

According to the records, the UNF and Cooper's office continued to renew the two agreements—and added a $315,980 grant for a third climate adviser in the state's Department of Transportation and a $144,949 grant for a fourth climate adviser in its Department of Commerce—through the end of his term in 2024.

In one of the office's final applications to renew funding under the initiative, it argued the positions would help "institutionalize Governor Cooper's climate legacy."

"The position will primarily focus on implementing and institutionalizing the Governor's priorities articulated in numerous executive orders and other directives," the application submitted in July 2023 stated. "This important work includes identifying and prioritizing federal funding sources that will most effectively further the Cooper administration's climate, clean energy, and environmental justice objectives."

The UNF-funded advisers, meanwhile, were evidently successful in pushing many of the policies outlined in the state documents. They were less successful, though, in shielding those policies from the legislature, which routinely overturned Cooper's most extreme policies with its veto-proof GOP majority.

Cooper's crowning climate achievement was 2021 legislation directing regulators to take "all reasonable steps to achieve" to slash carbon emissions from the state's electric power sector by 70 percent by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. The bill's 2030 mandate, however, was axed by a bill passed last year after the state's utilities commission determined it was "no longer reasonable or executable," the Associated Press reported.

Similarly, in 2021, the Cooper administration moved to enter North Carolina into the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, a multi-state program forcing utility companies to pay states for greenhouse gas emissions they are responsible for, something supporters say will drive emissions down over time, but critics say functions like a carbon tax and makes energy less affordable. The UNF-funded advisers were tasked with overseeing the process for joining the initiative. But in 2023, a veto-proof majority in the state's legislature passed a bill prohibiting the state from participating in such a program.

The Transportation Climate Initiative, the other multi-state emissions program the UNF-funded advisers sought to thrust North Carolina into, dissolved after several states withdrew from it over concerns about how it would drive gas prices higher.

In 2022, Cooper signed an executive order calling for half of all new car sales to be electric by 2030, a plan that closely mirrored California's EV mandate. Months later, he ordered his administration to adopt California's "clean truck" rules, forcing manufacturers to sell a progressively larger amount of electric trucks over time. That same order directed state agencies to transition their vehicle fleets to electric.

The North Carolina legislature eventually overturned the clean truck regulations and blocked agencies from prioritizing costlier electric vehicles.

Cooper further sought to prioritize offshore wind development and rewrite the state's building code to make it more energy-efficient and climate-friendly. Last year, the state's largest utility company backed out of its offshore wind plans after an independent review determined they were not cost-effective, and the developer behind the largest offshore wind farm proposed in the state agreed to forfeit its federal lease in April. In 2024, the legislature blocked Cooper's building code rewrite.

The U.S. Climate Alliance declined to comment on the specifics of its work in North Carolina and directed the Free Beacon to the governor's office. The North Carolina governor's office—now occupied by another ostensibly moderate Democrat, Josh Stein—did not respond to requests for comment.

"At a time when communities across the U.S. are being impacted by worsening climate-driven disasters—from hurricanes and floods to fires and droughts—it's critical our leaders, both Democrats and Republicans, have the resources they need to protect Americans and better prepare for what's to come," Evan Westrup, a spokesman for the initiative, said in a statement.

The alliance, which is now made up of 22 Democratic-led states and the Republican-led Vermont representing more than half of the U.S. population, has previously argued that states that participate in their programs are responsible for managing their own work. The North Carolina documents reviewed by the Free Beacon, however, show the group required the state to provide it regular status updates and withheld funding until receiving those reports.

In a statement, a spokesman for the Cooper campaign declined to address the UNF funding, but pointed to the former governor's record attracting business investment. "Roy Cooper recruited companies to our state to create thousands of jobs and put money in the pockets of North Carolina families while making North Carolina the best state for business three out of four years," the spokesman said.

Daniel Turner, the executive director of energy advocacy group Power the Future, said the documents suggest that Cooper was willing to let "globalist" powers influence his policymaking.

"North Carolina voters need to know their governor was purchased by globalist powers pushing a climate agenda which caused its energy crisis," Turner told the Free Beacon. "North Carolinians weren't Roy Cooper's priority. The United Nations was, and if as governor, he was doing the bidding of the U.N., who will be calling the shots if he's a senator?"

text:
The European Union is raising regulatory barriers to require that parts production and research and development take place in Europe, following additional tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles. The move marks a forceful response after Chinese EVs rapidly expanded their share to 15%. Support measures such as production subsidies have become urgent for South Korea's auto industry, which has no defenses against Chinese EVs.

Germany and France agreed on the 16th of this month to tighten "Made in Europe" standards to protect their auto industries, according to foreign media including Hong Kong's South China Morning Post on the 19th. Starting in 2028, the two countries will require vehicles to undergo final assembly in Europe and to source at least 70% of parts value, excluding batteries, from Europe in order to qualify for government support or public procurement benefits. European content will in principle be limited to the EU's 27 member states, though conditional exceptions may be allowed for non-member countries such as Britain and Norway.

The EU introduced countervailing duties on Chinese-made EVs in October 2024, to apply for five years. The additional duty rates are 17.0% for BYD, 18.8% for Geely and 35.3% for SAIC Motor, levied separately from existing general auto import tariffs. On the 9th, the EU agreed with China to cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 units a year, about half the current level.

While the EU is belatedly stepping up its defenses against Chinese EVs, South Korea remains close to unprotected. The tariff on low-priced Chinese EVs is just 8%, and EV purchase subsidies are effectively no different for domestic and imported models.

Chinese-made EVs accounted for 35.0% of the total in the first half of this year, underscoring how deeply they have penetrated the market. Even so, the government is moving to exclude EVs from the domestic production tax credit, known as Korea's version of the Inflation Reduction Act. "The United States and Europe are expanding incentives under an America-first or Europe-first approach," said Kim Pil-soo, a professor of automotive engineering at Daelim University. "It is time to secure the competitiveness of Korean-made EVs through tax credits and R&D funding support."

title: Amazon knows how to build big. The AI boom is testing just how big it can go. - Business Insider
description:
Amazon is committing hundreds of billions of dollars to data centers, servers, and power before investors know how quickly those investments will generate revenue.
Investors are concerned by the scale of the industry's expansion, especially as AI data centers are costing more to build and taking longer to complete.
However, the intensity of the AI data center building boom has made this type of coordination harder.
That puts pressure on the company to commit more money sooner to secure supply and meet its data center capacity goals.
It is managing a portfolio of commitments that can become more costly if a data center project is delayed.
text:
At an internal staff meeting in September, AWS CFO John Felton had a joke for Prasad Kalyanaraman, the executive overseeing much of Amazon's AI infrastructure expansion.

"You've taken us free cash flow negative as a company, so congratulations," Felton said, according to a recording of the meeting obtained by Business Insider.

The remark was lighthearted. But it captured a stunning reversal.

Just two years ago, Wall Street was debating what Amazon would do with its growing cash hoard. Now, cash flow has evaporated as Amazon embarks on its biggest bet ever, spending $220 billion this year alone to build the physical backbone for AI.

At the meeting, Kalyanaraman did not dispute Felton's premise. Amazon's machine-learning and AI business is "hugely free cash flow negative," he said, adding that he expects the company's free cash flow to remain negative for "the next couple of years or so."

Amazon has made big bets before. It spent heavily on cloud computing, fulfillment centers, and its delivery network long before they became some of the company's most valuable assets. Investors questioned those investments at the time, but Amazon ultimately built enormous, profitable businesses from them.

AI is testing this playbook at a far larger scale. Amazon is committing hundreds of billions of dollars to data centers, servers, and power before investors know how quickly those investments will generate revenue.

The company is the best, or among the best, at building data centers, with decades of experience. But the size and complexity of these projects, and the bottlenecks holding progress back, are challenging — even for such a respected cloud pioneer.

Internal documents reviewed by Business Insider and people familiar with the matter show the company trying to coordinate a sprawling industrial system whose parts move on different schedules. A delay in power, equipment, or construction can leave billions of dollars in hardware waiting — and Amazon's cash tied up — while forecasts and costs keep shifting.

Why Amazon thinks it will work

Amazon says it has strong evidence that the capacity will be needed. AWS revenue grew 37% in the second quarter, its fastest pace in 18 quarters, while its backlog reached $496 billion.

CEO Andy Jassy thinks the company has a "clear line of sight" to strong financial returns from this record investment cycle. In his latest annual shareholder letter, he called AI a "once in a lifetime opportunity" and said Amazon would not be conservative in its investments.

"We've been through this cycle with the first big AWS growth wave, and liked the results," Jassy wrote. "We expect to feel similarly about this next wave."

Investors are concerned by the scale of the industry's expansion, especially as AI data centers are costing more to build and taking longer to complete.

The market is "repricing anything that funds multi-year builds against revenue that arrives later," Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a recent report. Growing uncertainty around data center permitting and the political fight over electricity prices have given investors another reason to question how quickly these investments will pay off, he added.

Racks, but not enough power

One major industry challenge is securing enough power to run the equipment that goes inside data centers. This includes expensive racks of servers that contain GPUs and other chips that train and run AI models and services such as ChatGPT.

Internal emails from August show Amazon preparing a new "Early Rack Receipt" process for an expected wave of server racks carrying Nvidia's GB300 chips at US facilities before final deployment.

One Amazon email projected the company would take delivery of about $5 billion of Nvidia GB300 racks in August, followed by another roughly $3 billion each month "for the foreseeable future."

Some AWS data center sites had room for more racks but not enough available power to turn them on, people familiar with the effort said, leaving the equipment to be staged at intermediary warehouses until the facilities were ready. These people asked not to be identified discussing sensitive matters.

Timing and coordination

Usually, Amazon doesn't pay for racks until the gear is put into a data center, leaving suppliers to carry the cost of the equipment in transit, according to the internal documents obtained by Business Insider. This helps the company conserve cash.

However, the intensity of the AI data center building boom has made this type of coordination harder. Amazon has to compete more for scarce resources as it jockeys with rivals for access to Nvidia GPUs and other AI components.

Under the new "Early Rack Receipt" process, Amazon now takes ownership of these racks earlier in the supply chain, rather than waiting until the equipment reaches a data center.

The means spending cash sooner. And any delays getting the racks installed and plugged into a reliable power source potentially pushes back the moment when revenue starts flowing from these assets.

At least one AWS supply chain team did not have "a clear forecasted path" for getting racks into data centers, according to one of the emails reviewed by Business Insider.

An Amazon spokesperson said the company routinely stages finished hardware near deployment sites so it can be installed once power capacity is available, calling that approach "best business practice."

The spokesperson added that AWS has "long-established systems" to track infrastructure assets and disputed that the broader company lacks a forecasted path for getting racks into data centers.

This problem is not unique to Amazon.

Bernstein analysts wrote in a recent note that power permits, cooling systems, electrical equipment, construction, and hardware all move on separate schedules.

"Timing is imperfect," the analysts said.

"Inherently uncertain"

During the internal staff meeting in September, Felton, the AWS CFO, described the broader problem eloquently: "How do you work in the future when the future is inherently uncertain?"

Kalyanaraman, the AI infrastructure leader, said Amazon's internal outlook for the return on its AI investments had improved. But the assumptions behind those returns keep shifting.

"The forecast is changing on a daily basis," Kalyanaraman said. "The world that we live in is extremely dynamic."

Those shifting assumptions include when data centers will be ready and how much equipment AWS needs to keep on hand, he explained.

An eight-week supply buffer might be routine for a smaller company. But at Amazon's scale, Kalyanaraman said, this could mean holding "billions and billions of dollars" worth of additional equipment inventory — tying up precious cash.

Frugality meets the AI boom

Such tensions are especially striking for Kalyanaraman, a 21-year Amazon veteran who earlier this year was promoted to the elite S-team that reports directly to Jassy.

Amazon's founding story is defined by frugality. It famously used cheap doors as desks when founder Jeff Bezos started in Seattle in the mid-90s.

Kalyanaraman has absorbed this lore into bones. In late 2023, as AWS faced slower growth and layoffs, he urged employees to do more with less. "Frugality breeds innovation," he said back then.

That instinct still shapes his approach. In the September meeting this year, Kalyanaraman told Felton that AWS tries to make major investments at the "last responsible moment," when it has the clearest possible view of demand.

"If we can wait to spend the capital as late as possible, it's better for us," he said.

But the frenetic pace of the AI boom makes this principle difficult to follow. By the time demand is fully visible, the servers, power, and construction capabilities that AWS needs may no longer be available. That puts pressure on the company to commit more money sooner to secure supply and meet its data center capacity goals.

Kalyanaraman recalled telling Jassy in 2023 that AWS would "surely" be out of its capacity crunch by 2027. Instead, Amazon still expects demand to exceed its available capacity in 2027, the AI infrastructure chief said during the meeting this September.

Secured Power at Risk

Getting enough electricity may be the biggest challenge for an industry leader like Amazon.

The company has 44 gigawatts of data center capacity under development across 16 states, more than double Google, Meta, and Microsoft, according to Cleanview Research estimates.

An internal AWS dashboard called "Secured Power at Risk" tracks utility and regulatory constraints affecting electricity capacity AWS has lined up for its data centers.

The risks include transmission bottlenecks, requirements to reduce use during grid stress, and "use it or lose it" provisions that can jeopardize capacity if a data center project misses usage or construction milestones.

In other words, AWS is not simply waiting for electricity to arrive. It is managing a portfolio of commitments that can become more costly if a data center project is delayed.

Maryland proposals

A submission to Maryland's utility regulator last year, obtained through a public records request, illustrates the kind of exposure that can accompany massive data center buildouts.

Amazon told the Maryland Public Service Commission that large data center customers could help pay for grid upgrades or bring new power capacity to market without burdening other electricity ratepayers.

The company also proposed setting aside collateral to help utilities get more comfortable with the large investments needed to generate more electricity for data centers. Amazon proposed three years of collateral so that if a large electricity customer abandoned unused capacity, the utility would have time to re-sell the power.

The proposal is not evidence that AWS has made such a payment or posted collateral. It does, however, show that large data centers can face extra financial obligations, beyond their own electricity bills, if projects are delayed or cancelled.

The Amazon spokesperson said such utility rules are not unique to AWS. The company has not disclosed how much cash it has paid upfront to secure power.

New constraints 'keep popping up'

The AI buildout also incurs expenses that are harder to model than a conventional capex plan.

In the September meeting this year, Kalyanaraman said that while reviewing plans for gigawatts of capacity in West Texas, AWS confronted a labor problem: There weren't enough nearby pipefitters, electricians, and other skilled workers to build the facilities.

The company's response, he said, was to pay to construct housing complexes near its data centers so workers could live there for the two or three years needed to complete the projects.

Even the crates used to ship servers have become a planning issue. It may seem absurd to worry about the price of a container when servers cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, Kalyanaraman said. But at AWS's scale, where the company needs so many crates, even trivial items can become a material expense.

"We have new constraints that keep popping up," Kalyanaraman said.

title: How Syed Z. Islam is changing battery recycling - Oak Ridger

text:
He grew up in a rural village in the South Asian country of Bangladesh, helping to raise cows and goats and to plant, water and harvest rice, wheat, peas and tomatoes on land his father owned. He was only three months old and one of seven siblings when his father, an elementary school teacher, died in 1984.

“Our mother had no academic degree and as a woman was not allowed to hold a job,” Syed Z. Islam said. “My elder brother ran the farm. We grew up without electricity and running water. We lived in a two-bedroom bamboo house. We didn’t see tall buildings. We had no car.”

He endured beatings with a bamboo stick by teachers and his elder brother who wanted him to study harder. Because he became a good student, he was allowed to take science courses.

“Everybody wants to study science because of its opportunities to get good jobs,” he said.

Today, the Bangladesh native and U.S. citizen since 2024, is one of the most innovative researchers working at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. He has focused on devising separation technologies related to energy. Four companies (through six industry licenses) are commercializing these ORNL technologies. He has 13 patents and patent applications.

Islam is co-inventor with Ramesh Bhave of the ORNL membrane solvent extraction (MSX) process shown to be able to recover critical materials such as rare-earth elements from magnets in discarded smartphones, computer drives and many other devices, as well as lithium from end-of-life batteries from electric vehicles. The extracted rare earths and lithium can be reused for the manufacture of permanent magnets for new electronic devices and lithium-ion batteries respectively.

Islam earned a bachelor of science degree in chemical engineering from Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology in Dhaka, the nation’s capital.

“It is the Harvard or MIT of Bangladesh,” he explained of the university.

In Dhaka, he said, he first experienced the wonders of electricity, cars and tall buildings.

He and his future wife (by arranged marriage), who is a scientist, did so well on their graduate record examinations that they earned full scholarships after applying to several universities in the United States. He worked on a master’s degree in chemical engineering at North Carolina A&T State University in Greensboro, a historically Black college and university that gives scholarships to international students.

He said in an interview that he was “very excited to have the opportunity” to get a higher education in the United States and later to work at a national laboratory.

“Oak Ridge National Lab is one of the best places where I have worked, so I’m very happy here," Islam said.

He lives with his wife and daughter in Oak Ridge.

“I moved to ORNL in 2018 as a postdoctoral research associate after completing my Ph.D. in chemical engineering at the University of Kentucky,” he said. “That’s where I split water using sunlight to produce hydrogen gas that could fuel cars. At ORNL I do mostly translational research, which means solving practical problems rather than doing basic research.”

Islam, 42, is a separation scientist who leads a team of researchers at the Soft Materials and Membranes Group in the Polymer Chemistry and Separations Section of ORNL’s Chemical Sciences Division. He has received three ORNL Innovation Awards (2020, 2023, 2025) and an R&D 100 Award in 2024. R&D 100 awards are often referred to as the “Oscars of Inventions.”

In October 2025, he spoke to the Friday Lecture class of the Oak Ridge Institute for Continued Learning about his childhood and his innovations in a talk titled, “Energy-efficient Membrane Separations for Energy Technologies, from Concept to Commercialization.” Later, he was interviewed.

ORNL technologies Islam co-invented that have been licensed to industries for commercialization are “separation of high-purity copper using a scalable MSX process,” licensed to Camden Copper Holding LLC in 2026; “separation of critical battery materials from end-of-life sources,” licensed to Momentum Technologies in 2025; “forward osmosis composite membranes for concentration of lithium-containing solutions,” licensed to Element3 Resources in 2024; “separation of rare-earth elements using supported MSX,” licensed to Caldara Holding LLC in 2023; “recovery of critical elements from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries with supported MSX,” licensed to Momentum Technologies in 2020, and “separation of rare-earth elements using supported MSX,” licensed to Momentum Technologies in 2019.

“In addition to rare-earth elements, MSX showed high performance in recovery of battery materials such as lithium, cobalt and nickel from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries,” Islam said.

“Momentum Technologies in Texas is currently operating pilot- and demonstration-scale facilities using our membrane solvent extraction technology to recover lithium from discarded batteries.”

The method Islam, Bhave, Parans Paranthaman and others devised that received a 2024 R&D 100 Award was titled “Direct Lithium Extraction Sorbents.” Islam said it could be used to concentrate lithium chloride extracted from geothermal brine and other salty solutions. The ORNL technology was licensed to Element3 Resources for commercialization.

Islam and his colleagues have also been working on ways to capture carbon dioxide from the air to slow potentially devastating climate change and to improve sustainable aviation fuel made from wet municipal waste by removing nitrogen. Someday the novel technologies they develop to solve these problems may also be transferred to industry.
