As it gains steam, the push to electrify these vehicles could give the utility access to more stored energy, keeping ratepayers’ bills low, insulating fleets from the wild swings of diesel fuel prices, and (of course) help Oregoons Oregonians breathe a bit easier. Literally.

title: Weather in NJ is increasingly volatile. FEMA must be funded | Opinion
description:
"This isn't going to be the last nor'easter,” meteorologist Steven DiMartino of NY NJ PA Weather told Asbury Park Press journalists.
President Donald Trump’s federal funding cuts paused nearly $10 billion in FEMA disaster aid for nonprofits working to rebuild structures and rehouse people after climate disasters.
It means New Jersey families without specific flood insurance coverage will have to pay out of pocket to cover damage from this storm.
We can make our voices heard at the polls by voting for politicians who didn’t rubber-stamp Trump’s war in Iran, his gutting of clean energy and his FEMA cuts.
If congressional Republicans won’t listen to us while they’re in office, we can send a message this November by voting them out.
text:
Last month's nor’easter reminded me and many of my New Jersey neighbors of Superstorm Sandy and other bad storms we’ve weathered over the years. More than 100,000 people along the East Coast lost power, and parts of New Jersey saw more than 4 inches of rain by Sunday, Sept. 27.

As we reckon with the damage this recent storm caused, we’re also staring down the uncomfortable reality that there will be more where this came from.

"This isn't going to be the last nor'easter,” meteorologist Steven DiMartino of NY NJ PA Weather told Asbury Park Press journalists. “This is a first shot of many that is on the way. You have very warm waters out there, and any type of polar air mass that interacts with that warm water, with the right short wave that comes in, is going to lead to more coastal storm events, unfortunately.”

We cannot cut federal disaster funding. NJ needs it

Perhaps the worst part of all is that this string of nor’easters is coming as the government is letting Americans down across the board. It’s becoming more and more expensive to heat and cool our homes, fuel our cars and insure our houses, and on top of all of it, disaster relief is being slashed and denied.

President Donald Trump’s federal funding cuts paused nearly $10 billion in FEMA disaster aid for nonprofits working to rebuild structures and rehouse people after climate disasters. The Trump administration directly delayed emergency management funding to state and local agencies. Given that we can’t count on the government to help us after disasters, the burden is now placed on insurance companies — but home insurance is getting harder and more expensive to come by.

Standard homeowners’ insurance policies typically don’t protect against flooding, often forcing homeowners to purchase that protection separately. FEMA estimates that only 4% of homeowners across the country have flood insurance, even though 99% of U.S. counties have been affected by flooding since 1996. It means New Jersey families without specific flood insurance coverage will have to pay out of pocket to cover damage from this storm.

Between 2020 and 2025, home insurance rates in New Jersey rose by 32.1%. That’s a significant cost increase, especially given all of the other cost increases we’ve been hit with recently, many of which are the direct result of Trump’s policies. His unpopular war in Iran has sent gas prices skyrocketing, and the proliferation of data centers and gutting of clean energy production have sent electricity prices through the roof.

The Trump administration has canceled or threatened eight clean energy projects in New Jersey, jeopardizing 8,519 jobs, over $3.6 billion in investment, and 4.8 GW of clean energy being added to the grid. Meanwhile, Trump’s policies have raised costs for the average New Jersey household by more than $2,314 through the first half of 2026. Since Trump took office, household electricity costs in New Jersey have increased by 28%. From June 2025 to June 2026, residential gas prices in New Jersey increased by 9%.

Op-ed continues below gallery.

New Jersey needs better representation

Congressional Republicans may be trying to distance themselves from Trump’s cost-of-living crisis as the midterms approach, but most of them have rubber-stamped his agenda every step of the way. Which congressional Republicans stood up for New Jersey residents when Trump denied $227 million in aid requests for four Democratic-led states, including New Jersey, to recover from a major February 2026 snowstorm?

We deserve elected officials who will help us recover from disasters, just as we deserve to be able to fill up our cars or buy groceries without breaking the bank. But that’s not Trump’s plan. In May 2026, his FEMA Review Council recommended raising the threshold for disasters to qualify for federal assistance and shifting more financial and administrative burden for recovery and preparedness to states.

His tariffs are expected to make recovery efforts after disasters more expensive. The National Association of Home Builders estimates a cost increase of $10,900 per home due to tariffs on construction materials. Meanwhile, Trump’s attempts to undermine National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research and forecasting and cut disaster relief at the Department of Housing and Urban Development would also raise the cost of home insurance.

So what are New Jerseyans supposed to do, other than cross our fingers that the next storm isn’t worse than the last one? We can make our voices heard at the polls by voting for politicians who didn’t rubber-stamp Trump’s war in Iran, his gutting of clean energy and his FEMA cuts. If congressional Republicans won’t listen to us while they’re in office, we can send a message this November by voting them out.

Ed Zipprich is a former Red Bank councilman.

text:
Insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to cut the cost of living, create jobs and boost the UK’s economy than drilling for new oil, research suggests.

The government’s £15bn warm homes plan, currently under threat of cuts as ministers seek budget savings, would slash £1bn a year from household energy bills across the UK, concentrated on those on low incomes, according to research by the thinktank E3G. It would also provide a £1.6bn yearly boost to the economy, and about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses.

The Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, the analysis found. The jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of them – Equinor – an overseas investor.

A decision on whether to give the green light to the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea was “imminent”, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said on Wednesday. A decision on Rosebank would take a little longer, she said.

Labour promised in its 2024 election manifesto to halt new licensing for oil and gas, but Jackdaw and Rosebank could be exceptions because they were already in the licensing system.

Equinor previously estimated 3,500 jobs would be created at peak for Jackdaw and Rosebank combined.

Experts have repeatedly pointed out that new North Sea oil and gas would not bring down fuel prices or ease any supply constraints on the UK arising from the Iran war, because oil and gas are sold on international markets.

Some proponents of drilling argue that the economic boost to the UK and tax revenues for the government are reasons to grant licences. But related research by WWF and the campaigning group Uplift shows that tax revenues are likely to be limited, given the concessions that drillers can expect. While the total profits from Rosebank for its backers, Equinor, Shell and Ithaca Energy, could be £1.5bn over its 25-year lifespan, the UK government faces a potential loss of £258m through tax breaks and incentives.

Tax revenues from the North Sea were about £4bn in 2025-26, but upstream tax relief and support measures amounted to an estimated £3.26bn.

As the North Sea is a basin in steep decline, tax revenues from drilling are projected to fall to about £100m by 2030. Decommissioning costs for drilling platforms are also a major factor: taxpayers are likely to be asked for £12bn as the North Sea’s infrastructure is dismantled.

The warm homes plan, under which up to 5m homes would be insulated, would draw in a further £15bn in private investment, according to E3G, which would be spread across the country rather than concentrated in one area, in line with Andy Burnham’s pledge for economic growth “in every postcode”.

E3G also estimates that delivering the warm homes plan in full would boost GDP by 0.08%, while AI modelling suggests Rosebank would add about 0.025% on average through its lifetime, assuming the average oil price returning to $70 a barrel from recent highs. If the UK taxpayer paid for decommissioning, this would outweigh any positive impact.

James Huw Dyson, a senior researcher at E3G, said: “When the first cold snap rolls in, the public aren’t going to thank the government for cutting home insulation while giving big oil tax breaks to drill for polluting energy that keeps our bills high. If the government is serious about tackling the cost of living, and investing across the country, it should focus its attention on insulating homes and rolling out clean energy, which will cut bills and create good jobs across Britain at the same time.”

Ten major unions wrote to the government on Thursday to oppose granting a licence to the Rosebank oilfield. Scores of Labour MPs also oppose the move, and 600 scientists wrote to ministers over the summer urging a rethink.

Dhara Vyas, the chief executive of Energy UK, which represents the energy industry, said: “We need government to stick to its ambitions on electrification. Watering down the warm homes plan or making further changes to the zero emissions vehicle mandate sends mixed signals to a market that has been in a state of flux for far too long – these businesses cannot easily ramp up production again, and sadly for too many have already had to close.”

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero declined to comment on E3G’s findings or the future of the warm homes plan.

A spokesperson for Adura, the joint venture between Equinor and Shell that owns Jackdaw and Rosebank, said: “Analysis has shown that approving Rosebank and other planned North Sea oil developments would support £35.3bn in UK economic value between 2026 and 2035. Rosebank alone represents private sector investment of £8.7bn, three quarters of which will be spent in the UK, and together with Jackdaw will contribute £4.1bn in additional tax revenue over the next decade.”

These figures take in the company’s wider operations beyond Rosebank and Jackdaw, and also make assumptions about the wider supply chain and the spending of employees as economic benefits, which are uncertain. On the tax take, they do not take account of the large tax reliefs available, estimated at more than £2.4bn. Contrary to standard HM Treasury practice, Adura’s estimates do not appear to factor in a discount rate for future income.

text:
It may look futuristic, but the Lucid Air feels like a throwback to a time when all EVs were luxury cars that started at $70,000, because the tax credits would take the sting off. Thankfully, Lucid is getting with the times with some attractive lease offers.

You Can Hop Into A Lucid Air For $699 A Month

Lucid recently reported $1.4 billion in "cash flow improvement opportunities." To our untrained ears, that sounds like business-speak for "we need to make some darn money, fast." To that end, you can now lease a $70,900 luxury car at $699 a month.

Here's how the deal breaks down:

$699/mo for 36 months

$6,999 due at signing

Deal expires October 31, 2026

Offer available on a 2026 Lucid Air Pure

Qualifying lessees only

The (relatively) low price is made possible by one of two discounts: the California MyFirstEV Discount, and the Lucid Go Electric Credit for customers outside California. In either case, you're applying a $3,500 credit to the lease, but you can only claim one or the other. There's nothing in the fine print about not stacking discounts, but these two in particular are mutually exclusive.

The 620-hp Touring Is Only $120 More Per Month – And Worth Every Penny

The 620-horsepower Touring and 819-hp Grand Touring can also be leased. The Touring will have you paying $819 a month with $7,319 due up front, while the Grand Touring will have you paying $1,449 per month with $8,949 due up front.

If you ask us, the Touring model is the sweet spot. If you're already paying $699 to lease a base model, you're just shy of a 620-hp EV for another $120 per month. But leasing isn't the only way Lucid is trying to move metal – and the financing offer may actually be the more surprising play.

You Can Finance A Lucid Air At 0.00% APR

Leasing protects you from depreciation – but what if you actually want to own one of these things? Lucid's answer is 0% APR, which is an offer almost no luxury automaker makes. The lease offers covered above don't specify an offer to buy once the lease is up. If you want a Lucid Air to keep, you'll want to look at the finance tab, which has the Pure and the Touring advertised at 0% APR plus $2,500 in Lucid Credit. Here's how this deal works:

0.00% APR for up to 60 months

Deal expires October 31, 2026

Offer made on a 2026 Pure or Touring

Qualifying buyers only

Offer may be combined with other incentives, but not all incentives are combinable

The Lucid Air Grand Touring is available to finance at 2.99% APR, which is less than half the national average rate of around 6.3%. Here's what that loan might look like, assuming we're paying the whole thing off in five years.

This is before taxes, titling, and other expenses.The question is whether you would actually want to buy a Lucid Air at this price, even if you can get really low APR. Keeping an 819-hp supercar in your driveway sounds like fun, but EVs depreciate quickly, and your Lucid Air will be outdated by the time you pay it off. At this point, a used EV is a more sensible path to big electric horsepower.

The 2027 Lucid Gravity Can Be Financed At 1.99% APR

1.99% APR for up to 60 months

Stacks with up to $5,000 in Lucid Credit

Offer expires October 31, 2026

Qualifying buyers only

Offer may be combined with some, but not all other available incentives

Let's see what that loan would look like with a $20,000 down payment, assuming we can claim the full $5,000 in Lucid credit.

At these terms, our total cost actually comes out to less than MSRP because the $5,000 credit outweighs our $2,822 in interest.Realistically, very few buyers are going to qualify for this deal. But if Lucid is this desperate to move some product, that means this is a good time to buy, no matter what your credit looks like.

Used Lucids Are Already Selling At Half Price

The Lucid Air hit the market for the 2022 model year, and it's already lost quite a bit of value on the used market, with some listing for around half their MSRP. We dug up the following examples.

A 49,950-mile 2023 Touring is selling for $37,990 in Arizona.

A 17,206-mile 2024 Pure is selling for $35,084 in California.

A 17,377-mile 2023 Pure is selling for $34,984 in California.

A 39,334-mile 2023 Touring is selling for $41,590 in Illinois.

A 23,239-mile 2023 Touring is selling for $41,590 in California.

A 30,214-mile 2023 Touring is selling for $41,990 in Ohio.

A 30,030-mile 2023 Touring is selling for $41,990 in Texas.

A 10,985-mile 2022 Touring is selling for $53,990 in New Jersey.

A 10,044-mile 2022 Touring is selling for $52,590 in California.

There's something to be said for being a car's first owner and enjoying that new car smell. But Lucids depreciate so quickly that they're unlikely to be worth half their MSRP by the time you've paid them off.Considering the fact that EV batteries have turned out to last a lot longer than once believed, a used Air might make more sense if you're looking to purchase. On the other hand, leasing the car for a few years and then turning it in means not having to worry about depreciation, or obsolescence, in the first place.

text:

In January, 1949, two Volkswagen Type 1 Beetles arrived in New York City. Six years later, Volkswagen of America was founded. The original Beetle was cute in an ugly sort of way. It was under-powered and its heater was anemic, but it was cheap and that was enough for many Americans. In fact, Volkswagen made a number of self-deprecating commercials that celebrated its low price and its foibles. Here is one called “Keeping Up With The Kremplers.”

From The Beetle To The Rabbit

Eventually, the allure of an inexpensive car that traced its heritage to the 1930s began to fade. The company reluctantly made the transition to a new car called the Rabbit in the US. In 1978, Volkswagen took over a former Chrysler factory in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, where it made more than one million cars over the next ten years. At the time, it was the first foreign owned automobile factory in the US since the Rolls Royce factory in Springfield, Massachusetts closed in 1931.

For a while, Volkswagen attracted customers by positioning itself as a builder of performance cars. The Rabbit GTI was very popular. It was followed by the Sirocco and Corrado, which were less so. Soon, Japanese manufacturers built their own US factories in the US and began offering modern cars customers actually wanted.

In response, Volkswagen shifted its focus to diesel powered cars,. That worked for a while, until the Dieselgate fiasco. Today, its market share in the US is a dismal 3.2 percent — well behind both Nissan and Subaru.

Headwinds In The Marketplace

Volkswagen once earned lofty profits in China, but those days are gone. At home, the company is planning to close four factories in Germany and slash its workforce by 100,000 over the next four years.

Last week at the Paris Automotive Summit, Oliver Blume, the CEO of Volkswagen Group, told the press he now believes the US market could be key to reviving the company’s fortunes. That is despite the crushing tariffs imposed by the current administration, which the company say are costing it more than $5 billion annually.

“The US is one big growth opportunity for Volkswagen Group, and therefore we are investing heavily,” Blume said. “For Volkswagen, we also have in mind to enter the very attractive rugged SUV and pickup segment. The US market is of great strategic importance to the Volkswagen Group. Our growth strategy for the region is accordingly ambitious. We see the US, especially, as one stable market for the future, with stable profit pools.”

Ruggeder And Ruggeder

Every automaker who sells cars and trucks in the US is chasing the “rugged” theme. Their ads all feature dirt roads, sweeping vistas, and flowing rivers, as if every driver climbs Pike’s Peak and fords the Colorado River every day on the way to work. In this fantasy world, there are never any other cars on the road and every day ends at a remote campsite in the Grand Tetons.

VofA wants to capture a piece of that magic with the vehicles that are said to be coming from its Scout division. Plans for that division were announced in 2022, but production at its new factory in South Carolina is not expected to begin until 2028, at the earliest,

Audi is desperate to build its high profit SUVs in America, but has no US factory available. In theory, the Volkswagen factory in Chattanooga has spare capacity, now that production of the ID.4 has ended. Could it build its cars at the Scout factory in South Carolina? Nobody knows.

Blume also said Volkswagen wants to introduce a midsize pickup truck to compete against the Chevy Colorado, Ford Ranger, and Toyota Tacoma. Good luck with that. Truck buyers are the most brand loyal customers there are. Toyota has been trying to crack the full size pickup truck market in the US for thirty years, with limited success. Hyundai and Kia both plan to introduce new pickups to the US market by 2030, and Stellantis says it is bringing back the midsize Dakota pickup in early 2028.

Meet The New Boss

Former Audi sales chief Marco Schubert took charge of Volkswagen’s operations in North America on October 1, 2026. He is expected to create a plan to return the company to profitability within 100 days. Bloomberg says his biggest challenge may be the Byzantine bureaucracy at company headquarters in Wolfsburg, Germany.

Schubert faces a sclerotic decision making process, because Volkswagen Group is not a single automaker but a federation of fiercely independent brands. Audi, Porsche, and Volkswagen all have their own engineering cultures, product priorities, and power centers that compete for scarce financial resources. Executives in Wolfsburg have tried to impose common platforms and technology, with mixed success.

Some may recall when every General Motors division made its own engines and transmissions, which promoted innovation. However, the inefficiencies built into the procurement process cost the company dearly in squandered profits.

“There is probably a need for some humility on the part of the German management, just to really sit and listen and internalize what it is that the US market needs, because it’s not what other markets need,” Ed Kim, president of AutoPacific, told Bloomberg. “The market they’re trying to get into is very, very challenging and a very, very crowded space. It’s vastly different from Germany. It’s vastly different from China.”

Where Does Scout Fit?

Another conundrum Schubert needs to resolve is how to manage dealer expectations when its Scout vehicles are ready to go on sale. At the present time, Volkswagen wants to cut them out of the loop entirely and sell its Scout vehicles direct to the public the way Tesla and Rivian do. Not surprisingly, the company’s long suffering US dealers, who have seen their sales dwindle for decades, are none too pleased with that idea.

title: San Antonio Area Gets 24 New EV Charging Stations - Hoodline
description:
Twenty-four new electric vehicle charging stations are headed to the San Antonio area, with 21 of them landing inside the city itself and the rest split between Seguin and Hondo.
The 24 planned stations come out of Phase 2 of the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program, a federal effort established under the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, according to KENS 5.

text:
Twenty-four new electric vehicle charging stations are headed to the San Antonio area, with 21 of them landing inside the city itself and the rest split between Seguin and Hondo. The buildout follows the September opening of San Antonio's first EV fast-charging station on the city's southeast side, a Shell gas station at 418 Fair Avenue near Interstate 37.

The 24 planned stations come out of Phase 2 of the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program, a federal effort established under the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, according to KENS 5. That first phase has already opened 22 stations statewide, with at least five more expected by the end of the year and another 30 planned to open across Texas in 2027. Stations are also under construction in Wichita Falls, Selma and Kerrville.

The Texas Department of Transportation unlocked the next wave of funding after the Federal Highway Administration officially certified in January that the state had fully built out its Phase 1 network along designated Alternative Fuel Corridors, according to a document posted on the Texas Department of Transportation's FTP site. That federal sign-off is what allowed TxDOT to announce $226 million for 321 charging stations spread across 264 MPO areas and 57 county seats statewide.

Why San Antonio Qualified for 21 Stations

The money flows through Texas's 25 metropolitan planning organizations, bodies created under the Federal Highway Act of 1962 to oversee transportation planning and funding in metro areas, the station's report notes. Locally, the Alamo Area Metropolitan Planning Organization is responsible for all 24 stations planned across the San Antonio area, and it gathered input through three public workshops plus an online crowdsourcing application before sending its site recommendations to TxDOT.

“We are pleased with the results of this effort,” said Sonia Jiménez, deputy director of the Alamo Area Metropolitan Planning Organization, per the same account. TxDOT Data Management Director Michael Chamberlain said the number of alternatively fueled vehicles on Texas roads continues to rise, and that the new stations will help the agency keep pace with demand.

Federal NEVI rules require every funded fast-charging site to include at least four non-proprietary DC fast-charging ports, each capable of delivering at least 150 kW simultaneously, and to sit within a mile of a designated travel corridor, according to the Federal Highway Administration. Those standards are designed to let several drivers charge quickly at once rather than wait in line behind a single slow port.

EV Registrations Are Climbing Fast Statewide

The push comes as Texas's EV population keeps expanding. The state had 456,667 registered electric vehicles in February, a number that climbed to 532,282 by mid-October, according to TxDOT data cited by the same outlet. Texas received roughly $407 million in total NEVI formula funding over five years, the largest allocation of any state, per the Center for the New Energy Economy, with the federal grants covering up to 80 percent of project costs and private site developers supplying the rest.

That growth has a cost side, too. Under Texas Senate Bill 505, which took effect in 2023, EV owners pay a $200 annual fee at registration renewal and $400 upfront on new purchases, money that flows into the State Highway Fund, according to the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles. State agencies have estimated Texas loses roughly $200 a year in uncollected fuel taxes for every EV on the road, since those drivers skip the pump.

Grid Strain and Local Charging Options Already in Place

San Antonio's municipal utility, CPS Energy, is already working to keep the city's grid from buckling under rising EV demand. In June, the utility partnered with grid software provider WeaveGrid to launch the EV Smart Rewards program, which offers residential EV drivers up to $120 in annual bill credits plus a $30 enrollment incentive for charging during off-peak hours, according to WeaveGrid. The incentives encourage off-peak charging.

CPS Energy's FlexEV public charging network includes Level 2 stations, including one at an H-E-B. Those Level 2 ports typically add about 20 miles of range per hour of charging, a much slower pace than the high-speed NEVI chargers now being planned.

San Antonio adopted its SA Climate Ready plan in 2019. Bexar County continues to face federal clean air standards challenges tied to ground-level ozone.

title: Can Gulf Investors Make Sustainable Mining Their Edge in Africa?
description:
From Guinea’s bauxite sector to mining and infrastructure projects in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mauritania, Namibia and Morocco, Gulf investors and companies are active across the continent, with engagement already spanning mine ownership, financing and commodity trading.
Qatar-linked investors have also signaled interest in mining, energy, and infrastructure projects across the continent.
What the Gulf brings Gulf investors may hold distinct advantages, beginning with capital.
Gulf SWF capital can also move faster and with fewer conditions than much of Western development finance.
Yet Gulf capital is not unlimited: Domestic diversification priorities, geopolitical uncertainty, and project risk mean that African investments will still need to demonstrate commercial and strategic value.
text:
Critical minerals took center stage in global diplomacy this September. At the BRICS summit in New Delhi, whose 11 members include the United Arab Emirates, leaders called for “reliable, responsible, diversified, resilient, fair, sustainable, and just” critical mineral supply chains that preserve the sovereign rights of resource-rich countries. Ten days later, at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Secretary-General António Guterres launched a Country Support Mechanism to help resource-rich developing countries build domestic mineral value chains while strengthening environmental and human safeguards. Zambia, which has signed a mineral-cooperation memorandum of understanding with Saudi Arabia, is among the initiative’s first six partner countries.

As African governments seek more from mineral partnerships than finance alone, Gulf investors will secure durable access not merely through capital, but by embedding commitments that deliver shared value, including environmental and social performance, into investments from the outset.

Diversifying beyond oil

Critical minerals underpin electrification, grid expansion, batteries, and advanced manufacturing, placing them at the intersection of industrial policy, climate ambition, and geopolitical strategy. Demand for key energy minerals has continued to grow, while investment and refining capacity remain geographically concentrated, heightening concern over supply security, especially for copper. For Gulf states, securing access to these materials supports economic diversification and more resilient supply chains. Africa, which holds about 30 percent of the world’s critical mineral reserves, is therefore an increasingly important partner.

From Guinea’s bauxite sector to mining and infrastructure projects in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mauritania, Namibia and Morocco, Gulf investors and companies are active across the continent, with engagement already spanning mine ownership, financing and commodity trading. In 2024, UAE-based International Resources Holding (IRH) acquired a 51 percent stake in Zambia’s Mopani Copper Mines, with the Zambian state retaining the remainder. Saudi Arabia’s Manara Minerals, a joint venture between the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund and mining company Ma’aden, has explored investment opportunities in Zambian copper and nickel. Qatar-linked investors have also signaled interest in mining, energy, and infrastructure projects across the continent.

This Gulf presence is growing as Africa’s external finance landscape diversifies. Western development finance has tightened, and Chinese sovereign lending has declined from earlier highs, even though Chinese commercial involvement in African mining remains substantial. A wider pool of potential partners can increase African governments’ room to negotiate, not only over price and ownership, but over local processing, supplier development, jobs, transparency, and environmental safeguards. Zambia’s new local-content requirements illustrate how governments can use this shifting investment landscape to press for stronger domestic economic benefits.

The stakes

Mining reshapes land, consumes large volumes of water and can damage farming and freshwater systems, while the roads and power lines that serve a mine extend its footprint beyond a single site. When communities bear these costs, opposition and regulatory intervention can follow, eroding a project’s “social license to operate,” the local consent on which its stability depends. Zambia knows the stakes. In February 2025, a tailings dam at a copper mine in Chambishi suffered a catastrophic failure, releasing an estimated 50 million liters of acidic waste toward the Kafue River basin, which sustains roughly 60 percent of Zambia’s population. The incident triggered acute ecological damage, large‑scale disruption to water services and livelihoods, and raised serious concerns about long‑term contamination and health risks. The government ordered the mine’s owner to restore the river and compensate affected farmers, signaling likely elevated regulatory scrutiny and stronger expectations for tailings governance among investors and lenders, and illustrating how environmental damage can create political and commercial liabilities that persist well beyond the life of a single mine.

But foreign investment can cut either way. Where safeguards are weak, investors may reproduce damaging practices; where capital arrives with technology and stronger governance, environmental performance can improve—as seen in Chile’s copper sector, where early tailings regulations and continuous upgrades made foreign‑invested mines leaders in earthquake‑resistant, lower‑risk tailings storage. Agreements between governments can set expectations on local value, transparency, and environmental protection, but only if they include clear implementation mechanisms and accountability. Foreign investors can play a role here by influencing institutional expectations and practices in developing-country markets.

What the Gulf brings

Gulf investors may hold distinct advantages, beginning with capital. Gulf sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) are estimated to manage $4 trillion to $6 trillion, more than 40 percent of global sovereign-fund assets. SWFs account for more than 80 percent of the GCC’s outward investment, reflecting their central role in economic diversification and cross-border investment. This is state-linked capital with a potential to take a long-term strategic view, a useful fit for mining projects whose environmental and social risks may emerge long after the initial investment decision. Gulf SWF capital can also move faster and with fewer conditions than much of Western development finance. Yet Gulf capital is not unlimited: Domestic diversification priorities, geopolitical uncertainty, and project risk mean that African investments will still need to demonstrate commercial and strategic value.

While many investment frameworks have often placed greater emphasis on investor protection and resource access than on sustainable development, newer approaches are beginning to rebalance these objectives. Collaboration among investors, banks, and development finance institutions can reinforce this shift by establishing common environmental and social expectations across the mining lifecycle, particularly at the feasibility, design, and construction stages when the scope to avoid or reduce impacts is greatest. The principles underpinning the Gulf’s established Islamic finance markets may be starting to converge with sustainable investing frameworks, creating further grounding for a more integrated approach to projects and partnerships. This gives investors the opportunity to set conditions before committing capital.

Environmental and social commitments should be as contractual and measurable as financial ones. This means embedding targets, public reporting, and independent verification in shareholder agreements and financing terms, so that both investors and host governments can enforce them. It also means publishing baseline assessments and closure plans, and building benefit-sharing and accessible grievance mechanisms into project design in line with host-country law. Credible baseline assessments of biodiversity, water, land and livelihoods, and measurable targets for avoiding, reducing, restoring and, where necessary, compensating for impacts, can be incorporated into mine plans, shareholder agreements, financing terms and closure provisions.

A broader approach to protecting nature and people would also look beyond the mine itself, assessing how roads, power infrastructure, and other activities across the surrounding landscape and supply chain affect ecosystems and communities. Where projects affect landscapes shared by several operators, investors can support joint assessments and pooled financing for conservation, restoration, and community livelihood programs, helping ensure that individual projects contribute to healthier ecosystems and stronger local economies.

Gulf state-linked companies and investors also possess potentially relevant capabilities. Decades of operating in hot, water-scarce environments have built expertise in wastewater treatment, water reuse, energy efficiency, and large-scale infrastructure. When these capabilities are applied to mine design and operations, they could matter especially where mines compete with farms and communities for scarce water, including in arid mining regions such as Namibia or Morocco, as well as in water-richer regions, where treatment and reuse can reduce withdrawals and lower the risk of contaminated discharges. Mining’s high energy demand similarly creates room to pair projects with cleaner electricity and storage. In 2025, IRH signed a memorandum with its sister company ePointZero to decarbonize its operations, beginning with Mopani in Zambia. The announced work includes consideration of on-site renewable energy, grid optimization, intelligent infrastructure, water reuse, waste minimization, and sustainable sourcing. This early-stage commitment illustrates the types of measures Gulf-backed operators could embed at project level.

Turning capital into trust

text:
Andrew Forrest, billionaire chairman of mining giant Fortescue, is calling on the government to accelerate green approvals and turn climate ambition into real-world construction.

In the lead up to the Global Citizen NOW: Perth event this week, Forrest says key industry stakeholders should use the platform to help make a tangible difference towards clean energy in WA.

“Global Citizen NOW: Perth puts Western Australia’s experience in front of the world. We should use that platform to show what can be built here and take that ambition into COP31 (the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference),” Forrest told this masthead.

“You don’t deliver an energy transition by talking about it. You deliver it by the Government doing what it is elected to do and providing approvals in the best interest of Western Australians, then immediately getting on and building it.”

Forrest’s charity Minderoo Foundation is a presenting partner of the Global Citizen NOW: Perth event which was co-created by Perth local Michael Sheldrick.

The organisation has helped to raise more than $71 billion to end extreme poverty and has seen big names such as Beyoncé, Rihanna, Coldplay and Lady Gaga along with world leaders from Justin Trudeau to Ban Ki-moon get involved in Global Citizen events.

On October 19 and 20, Global Citizen NOW: Perth – an action summit – and Global Citizen Nights: Perth – a free show – will be held at the Perth Convention Centre with a goal to accelerate action on clean energy, electrification and global development.

The action summit will run across both days and bring together leaders from government, business, philanthropy, First Nations communities and civil society to secure commitments to help provide energy access to millions of people.

Forrest said his company Fortescue is building the renewable energy system in the Pilbara to power their mines.

“We’ve made a clear commitment: Real Zero by 2030, eliminating Scope 1 and 2 emissions from our Australian iron ore operations without offsets,” he said.

“This is about more than changing how one company operates.

“The world needs abundant, affordable energy. Reliable power gives people opportunity and gives regions like Western Australia the chance to build new industries and create jobs.”

Premier Roger Cook will be giving one of the opening speeches at the event about what it means for WA to be a State of Energy.

“Twenty years ago, the idea of world leaders gathering in Perth to discuss the future of energy and economic development would have seemed unlikely,” Cook told this masthead.

“Today, Perth sits at the centre of one of the most dynamic regions in the world, and the conversations taking place here matter not just for Western Australia, but for our region and beyond.

“Global Citizen NOW is bringing together the people who can turn shared challenges into investment and action.”

He said the event acted as an opportunity to highlight WA as the State of Energy and show how it is helping to drive the global energy transition while simultaneously creating jobs and opportunities at home.

“WA has built its prosperity by taking on big challenges,” he said.

“The next challenge is ensuring we capture the opportunities that come with the transition to a lower-emissions future and continue building the industries that will power our economy for decades to come.

“Global Citizen NOW is about bringing people together, forging partnerships and making sure WA continues to play a leading role in powering growth and helping power the world’s transition.”

title: She was building her dream home. Then came a data center's 'minor' power plant on a ...

However, Pacifico’s ability to receive a minor source permit hinges on the fact that it does not plan to operate the turbines year-round.

text:
BASTROP COUNTY, Texas — Merrie Saltana was three days away from pouring concrete for the foundation of her family’s dream home when she heard about the data center proposed across the street. It was late July, and she had hoped the home would be ready by Thanksgiving.

The contractor told her that might be a stretch, but definitely by Christmas, Saltana would be able to move in with her husband and their five youngest children. She had already picked a mesquite tree near what would soon become the front of the house to hang Christmas lights on.

Saltana and her husband are both from Austin, Texas and they chose the 3.7-acre property nestled among woody, gentle hills 40 minutes southeast of the city to enjoy a quiet life. They started looking for a property in 2018 while Saltana was still in the midst of an over two-decade career in the Army.

In 2022, they found it on the edge of a sparse rural community called Cedar Creek.

“Welcome to my little piece of Heaven,” Saltana told Straight Arrow from the shade of one of her trees on a warm October day. “For now.”

On that decisive day in July, Saltana saw a Facebook post for a community meeting hosted by the League of Independent Voters about local data center developments. It included a map of a newly proposed data center alongside its own dedicated power plant.

“It was like somebody punched me in the gut,” Saltana said. She called the contractor to put the concrete pour on hold.

The data centers supporting America’s AI boom are increasingly building their own dedicated power plants to speed up when they can begin operating, and attempt to prevent residents from seeing any impact on their electricity bill. This allows Big Tech to power the digital behemoths without waiting for connection to the broader grid where spare capacity for a data center is hard to come by. But many of these newly proposed power plants are receiving approval with minimal public participation before a facility is built by finding ways to fit into regulations written for small-scale facilities.

In Texas, where a critical mass of new data centers are proposed, a Straight Arrow analysis of air permit data found a surge in applications under a less rigorous “minor source” process.

As a result, communities across the country are finding themselves on the front lines of new sources of air pollution that government regulatory agencies consider safe on paper. Yet environmental groups and many residents worry about the cumulative effects of new facilities that they believe are being rushed.

“There’s a big risk for air pollution to be worse than it would be if these were more regulated and if these projects had more oversight,” said John Bangsund, director of science and technology at the Better Data Center Project, a nonprofit that provides expertise to communities affected by data center development.

What are the permit requirements?

When a company wants to build a power plant or other potential source of air pollution, it goes to state environmental agencies for relevant permits, known as a New Source Review. Those agencies follow the federal Environmental Protection Agency rules, which classify facilities seeking permits under the Clean Air Act into major and minor sources of new air emissions.

The major or minor distinction is a regulatory threshold based on how much pollution a facility has the potential to emit into the atmosphere. The purpose is to ensure a higher regulatory standard for facilities that can produce large amounts of emissions known to harm human health. There are specific caps for particulate matter — microscopic particles that can enter the lungs, causing asthma and cardiovascular issues — and other chemical compounds known to raise an individual’s cancer risk or destabilize the Earth’s ozone and climate systems.

A power plant permit classified as a major source is subject to public comment periods, and the public is able to request a hearing. Major sources also need operating permits known as Title V in addition to New Source Review, which provides additional opportunities for the public to weigh in.

The extent of public engagement for power plants classified as minor sources can vary by state, but it generally provides fewer opportunities for the public to express concerns.

“There’s been a lot of regulatory developments over the past decades that have slowly chipped away and narrowed the scope of what is major,” said Surbhi Sarang, a senior attorney with the Environmental Defense Fund. “It’s allowed for a lot of loopholes and problematic determinations about what’s major and minor.”

The new power plant in Cedar Creek is proposed under a minor source process by claiming the power plant turbines will only run for a limited number of days throughout the year.

The minor permit classification can be misused, according to environmental groups, when those limits are violated or if multiple projects cluster together in one area despite technically having separate permits.

Kathryn Guerra, a campaign director for the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen who focuses on Texas’ environmental regulatory agency, said once a facility needs operating permits, it may reach the major source classification, triggering a public process.

“That’ll be the first opportunity that folks actually have to opine on the facility’s emissions. But the facility’s built,” Guerra said.

‘Bring your own power’

One example of what watchdogs call “permit segmentation” comes from Licking County, Ohio, where Meta’s Prometheus data center is expected to consume one gigawatt of power. That amount of electricity can power roughly 700,000 homes — more than enough for all the housing units in the cities of Columbus and Cleveland combined.

A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment on the record.

Meta’s subsidiary Sidecat LLC is contracted with Will-Power OH, part of the power infrastructure developer Williams Companies, to build and operate new gas power plants and batteries that will keep the Prometheus data center running.

The Williams power facilities are behind-the-meter, meaning they will connect to the data center but not the larger power grid, according to filings at the Ohio Power Siting Board obtained by Straight Arrow. Will-Power OH has filed four separate minor source applications for power plants adjacent to Meta’s Prometheus site.

Kyle Tarpley, a spokesperson for Williams, told Straight Arrow any claims that the company “avoided regulatory review are flatly wrong.”

Williams shared information with “local stakeholders” throughout the process and the applications underwent “Ohio EPA review, public notice, public comment opportunities and are subject to enforceable permit requirements,” Tarpley said. “Earning trust in the communities where we operate is just as important as meeting technical and regulatory requirements.”

Public meetings were held regarding the permit applications individually, but Bangsund said the cumulative impact was “deemed irrelevant.”

“None of these projects are being considered holistically,” said Bangsund, who has spent months digging through permit applications for power units attached to data centers. That research turned into a report released this month and co-published by the Better Data Center Project and environmental law nonprofit Earthjustice.

The report found 177 gigawatts of gas power plants proposed for data centers — enough to power 65% of all homes in the U.S. While Bangsund said most of the projects he has tracked file for major source permits, he has found that when the tech industry can find a way to fit the minor source category, it saves time in the regulatory process.

“By taking things behind the meter, by building them on their own, and by making them a little smaller, they’re just speeding that all up,” Bangsund said.

The power plant in the neighborhood

In Texas, the state regulatory agency, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), refers to minor source permits for New Source Review as a standard permit.

The standard permits for gas-powered electric turbines can be issued for any industrial facility, manufacturing or even major retailers like Walmart. However, a Straight Arrow analysis of initial standard permit applications received by TCEQ found a surge in 2024 and 2025 — the same years in which the data center boom began to take hold.

From 2016 to 2023, TCEQ received about 30 to 90 standard permit applications for new electric generation units per year. In 2024 the agency received 122, followed by 158 in 2025. As of mid-October, TCEQ has received 96 standard permit applications for new electric units in 2026.

In Bastrop County, the data center proposal in Saltana’s neighborhood is being built by BlackChamber, a Washington, D.C.-based digital infrastructure company. Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the chatbot Claude, will be the main user of the data center, the Austin Business Journal reported.

Neither BlackChamber nor Anthropic responded to requests for comment.

For constructing the onsite power plant, California-based Pacifico Energy filed a standard permit application with TCEQ in August. If approved, Pacifico will build 48 gas-fired turbines capable of producing 1.3 gigawatts of electricity. The turbines are similar to jet engines enclosed in a shell that can vary in size from a truck trailer to a small building.

Site plans reviewed by Straight Arrow show those 48 turbines on the north side of Earl Callahan Road, the opposite side of the street from one edge of Saltana’s property. She estimates the gas power generating units will be less than half a mile from her property.

Amy Fisher has lived in the neighborhood for 40 years and used to ride her horses around Earl Callahan Road with its two near-hairpin turns and gentle slope surrounded by ranch pastures. It was only a few years ago, by Fisher’s memory, that the road was paved.

A roadside meeting

On an October afternoon, Saltana, Fisher and five of their neighbors met on the side of Earl Callahan Road to discuss the project. They sat in lawn chairs and passed around bottles of water under a Texas sun emanating the last gasps of summer heat. So far, the only changes in the neighborhood were the surveying flags on the project site fluttering in a mellow breeze.

“I feel very dependent on these guys that are so knowledgeable and are really doing all the hard work,” Fisher said, gesturing to the rest of the group. Several have become unlikely experts in Texas’ regulatory process and have traveled to Bastrop County Commissioners Court meetings to speak up against the data center and power plant.

“I’ve been drinking from a fire hose to try to understand,” said Cameron Allen, a Cedar Creek resident.

Because the standard permit for electric generating units does not require public notice or a public comment period, Cedar Creek residents have limited ability to challenge the power plant in their backyard. The neighbors had to file a public information request to receive information on the Pacifico permit.

In terms of capacity to generate electricity, Pacifico’s turbines will be on par with the largest nuclear reactor units in the U.S. However, Pacifico’s ability to receive a minor source permit hinges on the fact that it does not plan to operate the turbines year-round.

Pacifico Energy did not respond to numerous requests for comment from Straight Arrow.

According to a data table in Pacifico’s permit application, the company will use six different turbine models, each with its own specified hourly operation totals between 2,648 and 7,028 hours per year. In other words, each of the six turbines will run somewhere between 30% and 80% of the hours in a non-leap year.

A ‘synthetic’ permit

Setting a limit on how often new power plant units will run is a common practice to stay under the emissions limit for a minor source permit. That practice, combined with some form of segmentation, is already leading to lawsuits.

Public Citizen and the Sierra Club filed suit last month against Vantage Data Centers over its project in San Antonio, about a 90-minute drive from Cedar Creek. The claim alleges that Vantage Data Centers and the power company VoltaGrid LLC split the backup power generators into two minor source permits that collectively exceed the emissions limit and should be categorized as one major source permit.

In North Carolina, the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC) is challenging the permit for Amazon’s 592 diesel generators at Amazon Web Services’ Energy Way Tech Campus, as well as a permit for 57 diesel generator units filed by Duke Energy. The environmental law group argues these should be considered one major source and asked the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality (NCDEQ) to hold a hearing at which they can argue that the permits should not have been granted.

“All of these generators are going to be on the same property and serving no other purpose other than powering Amazon’s facility,” said Caroline Cress, a senior attorney at the SELC.

Amazon’s generators on their own could exceed the minor source limit if not for the fact that the company agreed to cap how often they will run. Accepting an enforceable cap to slip under the major source threshold is called a “synthetic” minor permit.

“It really seems just like a sham way to get out of these requirements that are intended to protect local communities,” Cress told Straight Arrow. “If they have the choice between actually shutting down to avoid exceeding their limit versus just exceeding the limit and paying penalties, I think in a lot of cases they’re probably going to choose to exceed their limits.”

Duke Energy disagrees with SELC’s conclusion and is arguing against the nonprofit’s push for a hearing.

“The facilities were appropriately considered separate sources for Clean Air Act permitting purposes,” said Lee Friedman, a Duke Energy spokesperson. Friedman told Straight Arrow that the emissions would remain “below the strict permit requirements set to keep the public and surrounding environment safe.”

An Amazon spokesperson said the company expects the backup generators to run fewer than 10 hours per year and use the cleanest diesel technology designated by the EPA.

“Amazon appropriately applied for and obtained an air permit for our data center project,” the spokesperson told Straight Arrow. “We’re committed to protecting air quality in Richmond County and will continue to work closely with the agency to ensure we meet all applicable environmental and public health standards.”

The NCDEQ declined to comment due to pending litigation. But when the department issued the permits in August, its press release described the public process, which included a 30-day comment period. A public meeting also occurred in July.

“The two permits serve different purposes on different time horizons,” the NCDEQ said, noting that Duke Energy’s generators are “bridge power” while the data center awaits a grid connection, and Amazon’s generators are for emergency backup.

Duke Energy’s permits are valid only for a year, Friedman said.

Are regulatory agencies up to the task?

The key question for environmental groups monitoring state regulatory agencies is who ensures power companies are held accountable to the emissions limits outlined in their permit applications.

“It’s the honor system,” Guerra said, referring specifically to developers using minor permits in Texas. “They can do essentially whatever they want as long as on paper they represent that they’re in compliance.”

Bangsund’s report with Earthjustice and the Better Data Center Project paints a grim picture for health outcomes if all 177 gigawatts of gas power plants are built across the nation. The report estimates it could lead to $5.6 billion per year in healthcare costs due to health conditions related to air pollution. He expects Texas and Ohio to be two of the hardest-hit states.

Bangsund acknowledges that the current estimate could be too high because not all of the power plants are likely to be built. On the other hand, he said, “it might be conservative because this lack of oversight we’re talking about could lead to them emitting more than is in their permitted limit.”

In at least one case documented by the Lufkin Daily News, a TCEQ reviewer directed a company filing an application on behalf of a data center to revise its estimates for particulate matter emissions to fall just one decimal point below the major source threshold after its initial application exceeded that limit.

TCEQ did not provide comment to Straight Arrow.

‘Sand in the gears’

On the side of Earl Callahan Road, neighbors told Straight Arrow they have grown frustrated with the process.

“We want to bump it up to a major permit,” said Fred Heckeroth, who flies a handmade white flag on his dusty, two-door pickup. It reads “power plant” on one side and “data center” on the other; each is struck through with a bold red X. “It should go to that criteria and not on this lower level criteria.”

Allen, his neighbor, agrees. And he’s ready to take action.

“Part of our methodology has been to throw sand in gears and just slow this thing down,” he said. A major source permit provides more avenues for that.

As of mid-October, the permit for Pacifico Energy is still pending. And TCEQ is in the midst of a pause on data center approvals while Texas’ grid operator and the state commission regulating electric utilities audits a pipeline of projects looking to connect to the grid. The audit is expected to wrap up in December.

Nevertheless, the power plant and data center campus are looking to move forward with the first phase of construction at the end of November, according to reporting in the Austin Business Journal, which cited a filing with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

Neighbors are split on whether they would remain or move away if the project is built.

“We’ve come out here with this really beautiful goal of establishing exactly what we want for our lives, for ourselves, and for our kids,” Allen said. “The idea of having to run that whole thing back seems really tragic.”

And the group isn’t wholeheartedly against data centers. At first, Saltana wasn’t so alarmed.

“Being in the military for so many years, I know the importance of that infrastructure,” Saltana said. “Then I started digging a little bit more and peeling those layers of the onion.”

For Saltana, the problem is the scale of the data center and power plant and its proximity to the neighborhood where she had hoped her kids would grow up and play backyard soccer. She already sold her previous home to buy the property in Cedar Creek.

To ensure they had time to work on building their home, Saltana stopped taking clients for her accounting business. Her husband cut the number of projects he took on at his home renovation business. She estimates they’ve spent about $100,000 already on the property, including installing a septic system.

Now, she feels stuck.

Even if she decided to sell the property and move on, she faces a massive what if:

“Who’s gonna want to buy next to a data center, especially this type of data center next to a power plant?” Saltana asked.

title: Von der Leyen: EU needs whole puzzle of actions for lowering energy prices
description:
Von der Leyen reiterated the core climate pledges: replacing foreign fossil fuels with affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources and electricity.
The two-day negotiations between EU institutions and member states in Brussels were “long and dense,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged.
“We need a whole puzzle of actions,” Von der Leyen pointed out.
Gas prices have risen 140% since late February, and diesel prices have doubled, Von der Leyen said.
Von der Leyen highlighted the 80 GW of renewables capacity installed last year.
text:
The European Union is rolling out a range of measures against the surge in energy prices, including the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel and extending the temporary state aid framework, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said after the meeting of the European Council. EU leaders are yet to agree on a more comprehensive joint approach to the energy crisis and the tradeoff with carbon pricing. Von der Leyen reiterated the core climate pledges: replacing foreign fossil fuels with affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources and electricity. “We need a whole puzzle of actions,” she pointed out.

The two-day negotiations between EU institutions and member states in Brussels were “long and dense,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged. Speaking alongside European Council President António Costa after their latest summit, she said “there is no silver bullet” for the energy crisis as all countries have different energy mixes.

“We need a whole puzzle of actions,” Von der Leyen pointed out. She noted that since the start of the war in the Middle East, costs for imported fossil fuels have increased by EUR 106 billion, without a single additional molecule of energy. Gas prices have risen 140% since late February, and diesel prices have doubled, Von der Leyen said.

The EU is releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves

The EU is releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves over the next four months. In addition, it is extending in scope and time the temporary state aid framework introduced in February for vulnerable segments of industrial production. Another recent response with short-term effect was to postpone the Methane Regulation, for monitoring emissions for imported oil and gas, until January 2028.

Von der Leyen noted that the European Commission is opening a strategic dialogue on European refineries, mainly to have more of them operating. Such facilities have been cutting capacity and closing down for years. Their profit margins have especially narrowed or even went negative in the past few months. It all translates to a greater dependence on fuel imports.

Transition from imported fossil fuels toward nuclear, renewables is essential

The heads of state and government and top EU executives didn’t find much common ground on the longer-term path forward regarding the tradeoff between climate objectives and expensive energy. For the joint statement, they decided to stick with the core climate pledges from the programs of the previous administration such as REPowerEU, Fit for 55 and the European Green Deal.

“As long as Europe depends on imported oil and gas, our prosperity remains exposed to events beyond our control. This is why it is so important to stay the course of the transition that is a transition towards affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources – nuclear and renewables. We must change the way we consume energy, that is replacing foreign fossil fuels by electricity produced in Europe,” Von der Leyen stressed.

The European Commission’s chief said the grid has to be modernized and improved. Von der Leyen highlighted the 80 GW of renewables capacity installed last year. Six times more is waiting for network connection approval, she asserted.

Member states have specific individual circumstances

The current situation urgently requires a coordinated European response of targeted and temporary measures, taking into account the member states’ specific circumstances and safeguarding the single market, the European Council underlined.

The body welcomed the initiatives of the European Commission to bundle energy demand voluntarily, for joint purchases.

The energy transition remains the most effective strategy for achieving Europe’s strategic autonomy, strengthening resilience and structurally lowering energy prices, the European Council said

“Recalling the overarching imperative of reducing the EU’s dependence on volatile fossil fuel markets, the European Council stresses that the energy transition remains the most effective strategy for achieving Europe’s strategic autonomy, strengthening resilience, structurally lowering energy prices, and delivering the clean, abundant and homegrown energy needed to power the economy of the future, by accelerating electrification and deploying renewable and low-carbon energy sources, grids and energy storage, as well as fostering energy efficiency,” the conclusions read.

The European Council said the legislative process on the Market Stability Reserve should be accelerated with a view to moderating price

volatility. It is a mechanism within the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) designed to fix imbalances between the supply and demand of carbon emission allowances – EUAs. They can be pulled from the market or released back to ease price movements.

In the context of the ongoing review of the ETS system and to support European industrial competitiveness, the European Council repeated that a well-functioning, transparent and predictable carbon market is necessary to effectively protect against carbon leakage, to reduce the volatility of the carbon price and mitigate its impact on electricity prices, while preserving the essential role of the ETS in the climate and energy transition through a market-based price signal for carbon emissions that drives investment and innovation.

The most urgent matter, though, is an agreement on the 27-member bloc’s 2028-2034 budget, needed by the end of this year.

Eurelectric: Beyond short-term response, any measure must be targeted, temporary

In a response to the European Council’s update on energy and climate policy, Eurelectric – Union of the Electricity Industry commended the short-term measures to ease the pressure on bills.

But it pointed out that any further measure must be targeted and temporary, so it does not disrupt the market signals that drive investment.

“Europe must keep its industry competitive while unlocking the investment needed for affordable, secure and decarbonised energy. Eurelectric’s message to leaders is clear: electrification delivers both,” the statement adds. Mirroring the conclusions from the meeting, the association said the energy transition remains the most effective way to lower prices for good and secure Europe’s energy.

There was little word in the European Council about ETS 2 and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Eurelectric said policymakers need to implement ETS 2 rather than reopen it, backed by strong enabling policies and funding instruments like the Social Climate Fund. Early, targeted use of its revenues would protect vulnerable households and give investors certainty.

SolarPower Europe calls for making electrification affordable

SolarPower Europe highlighted the need to ensure a level playing field between electricity and gas. It argued that fairer energy taxation and a strong, predictable carbon price are essential to making electrification the affordable choice.

“Faster deployment of rooftop solar is a proven and swift solution for lowering citizens’ energy bills, while large-scale batteries can store cheap abundant renewable electricity and push out expensive gas peakers when electricity demand is high. These are practical, easy-to-deploy measures that can help shield European households and businesses before next winter,” Deputy Chief Executive Officer Dries Acke said.

text:
Xcel Energy is proposing to keep electricity rates flat for two years as Minnesotans’ complaints about rising utility costs mount.

The state’s largest electric utility says under the plan, filed with the state Public Utilities Commission last week, it would postpone any requests to raise its electricity rates until at least November 2028.

In exchange, Xcel wants permission from state regulators to use federal tax credits from planned battery storage projects sooner than expected.

Xcel expects to receive those credits from the federal Inflation Reduction Act for five battery projects near the retiring Sherco coal plant in Becker, at its Blue Lake facility in Shakopee and in Nobles County.

Xcel says the plan would allow it to continue to invest almost $4.5 billion in Minnesota’s electric system over the next two years, and help offset rising costs.

“This request demonstrates Xcel Energy’s commitment to keeping rates stable today while continuing to deliver safe, reliable electric service and make investments that power tomorrow,” said Bria Shea, president of Xcel in Minnesota, North and South Dakota, in a news release.

The proposal comes as state regulators examine the cost of electricity at a time when many Minnesotans are struggling to pay their utility bills.

Xcel's most recent rate increase, which state regulators approved in June, was 5.8 percent over two years. That proposal generated thousands of comments opposed to the increase.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and consumer advocates asked the Public Utilities Commission to reconsider the decision, but it declined.

Instead, it launched a statewide investigation to examine the affordability of electric and natural gas service provided by regulated utilities, including Xcel.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerous Pfas compounds – Pfoa and Pfos.

The EPA has found that virtually no level of exposure to either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies Pfoa as “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoa has been found to leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m plastic containers annually used across the US economy.

The containers present an “ongoing serious and ongoing threat to public health,” said Kyla Bennett, a former EPA scientist who is now science policy director with the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (Peer) non-profit.

Inhance has denied that the chemical leaches out in measurable levels, and told The Guardian in a statement that any Pfoa from its products are an “impurity”

The “phase-out” was put in place after documents made public during landmark early 2000s litigation on DuPont’s Pfas pollution in West Virginia laid bare the ubiquitous chemicals’ dangers and serious health risks. In 2015, facing intense pressure to act, the EPA reached an agreement with eight Pfas producers to “phase out” production of Pfoa and Pfos, a similar chemical produced by 3M.

Though the agency stopped short of a ban, the “phase out” was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution. Officials often repeated the claim that the chemicals had been phased out, giving the impression that they were no longer produced or used in the US.

Last month, the EPA quietly changed wording on its website that claimed Pfoa and Pfos had been phased out.. In fact, both have been produced in the US this whole time, and at levels that independent science suggest are quite high.

The EPA site previously stated: “The manufacture and import of Pfoa has also been phased out in the United States.”

It now reads: “Quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported, and used by companies … ”

The change was made in response to a complaint filed by Peer, which pointed out that the EPA was allowing Pfoa to be produced in the US. Under the Information Quality Act, data and information made public by federal agencies be complete and accurate.

“They were giving the false impression and saying, ‘Nothing to see here because Pfoa is not being produced in the US,’” Bennett told the Guardian. “But that was demonstrably false, and now they have admitted it.”

An epidemiological panel convened during the West Virginia DuPont case found Pfoa and Pfos likely causes cancer, heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease. The panel’s findings were the scientific basis for the phase-out.

The EPA did not immediately provide a comment to the Guardian. Inhance in its statement to The Guardian stressed that there was never a ban in place and it was not one of the eight companies that agreed to stop producing Pfoa.

The reversal underscores why phase-outs are inadequate, and the EPA needs to put in place bans, Bennett said.

“If you have a chemical and there’s no safe level of it, then why on earth would you allow it to be manufactured?” she said. “This all makes perfect sense if you understand the reality that the EPA is an arm of industry, especially under the Trump administration.”

The EPA’s reversal marks the latest twist in a six-year legal battle over Inhance’s Pfoa-infused containers.

The EPA seemed unaware that Pfas were being added to plastic containers until late 2020 testing by Peer found high levels of Pfas in pesticides stored in Inhance bins. The subsequent EPA investigation unearthed wide-scale contamination of plastic containers, prompting the agency to subpoena Inhance for information.

It publicly reminded the plastics industry that companies must submit for a safety review if they manufacture Pfoa. Inhance dismissed the agency’s evidence and claimed its containers did not leech Pfoa, but the EPA disagreed, again ordering Inhance in March 2022 to “immediately cease” production.

Two weeks later, Inhance put out a press release stating that its products did not “impart” Pfoa, and it did not cease production.

Subsequent EPA testing found the containers still contained Pfoa. Facing legal pressure from Peer, the EPA by December 2023 again ordered Inhance to stop making the containers. That ban was overturned by a federal appeals court. Peer later sued, but the case was dismissed because a federal judge ruled that the group lacked standing.

In its statement, Inhance said that it made adjustments to reduce by 90% the level of Pfoa “impurities”.

“Published peer-reviewed third-party risk assessments conclude that estimated exposure does not present an unreasonable risk to human health or the environment,” Inhance chief operating officer Patricia van Ee wrote. “We have shared our process data with EPA throughout its review.”

The EPA appears to have given up on enforcing the phase out and legally pressuring Inhance. Still, the EPA maintained on its website that Pfoa had been phased out of production, drawing the formal complaint from Peer.

In a response dated 18 September, EPA assistant administrator for chemical safety and pollution prevention, Douglas Troutman, wrote: “In response to Peer’s request, the EPA is updating its websites.”

The update also notes that Pfos is in US production in some “limited, ongoing uses”.

“This rare touch of candor by EPA is welcome, but it does not address the free flow of toxic Pfas saturating our food, water, and soil,” Bennett said. “Now that EPA has admitted that these two legacy Pfas are still manufactured in the US, it is past time to take effective enforcement action.”
